text:
Leonel Morocho Arteaga had just left the house when he noticed three black vehicles with tinted windows, he said in a sworn affidavit filed in federal court this week.

It was Aug. 26, the third day of an operation by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Danbury, where Morocho Arteaga lives, that resulted in dozens of arrests. But he didn't think much of it, he said in the affidavit — an appeal of his asylum case was still pending. They were probably there for someone else.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It wasn't until after Morocho Arteaga put his 6-year-old son on the school bus and returned to his parked car that he realized the agents were there for him, the affidavit continued. The three black vehicles he'd seen earlier encircled his car, and officers asked him to confirm his name.

"They never told me who they were, whether they were police or ICE, but I could see that they had the letters of ICE on their uniform," Morocho Arteaga said in the affidavit.

After the agents confirmed Morocho Arteaga's identity, he said one opened his door and grabbed him by his shirt.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"I told the officer who spoke Spanish to be calm (and) that I would go with them," Morocho Arteaga said in the court filing.

Morocho Arteaga's arrest was one of 118 across Connecticut during the four-day operation, according to ICE. It has drawn national attention as Democratic state and federal officials have said this was an example of ICE targeting someone at a bus stop. ICE, and its parent agency, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, did not return a request for comment for this story. In a statement to CT Insider for a previous story about this arrest, DHS denied the arrest took place at a bus stop.

“Any claim that ICE targeted parents at a school bus stop is FALSE,” the statement said. “The vehicle stop did not take place in the vicinity of a bus stop, and Morocho-Arteaga was alone.”

Video published by CT Insider on Monday appears to show ICE arresting an adult at an intersection moments after children get on a school bus less than a block away. The video was recorded by cameras attached to a Danbury school bus and was obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

While ICE does not have automatic permission to enter a school under the state's Trust Act law, arrests at or near bus stops in public places are allowed. That said, ICE has faced significant criticism for similar actions in the past.

In the new court filing, Morocho Arteaga gives his own account of the arrest and his subsequent detention. It's attached to an amended petition filed in the federal district court for Connecticut filed late Monday night in which the 28-year-old Ecuadorian citizen and father of two — whom ICE released from custody the same day it arrested him — asks the court to bar the agency from detaining him again and stop requiring him to wear the GPS ankle monitor it fitted him with upon his release, among other measures.

Morocho Arteaga's attorney, Mary Foden, of the Hartford-based firm De Castro Foden LLC, did not return a request for comment Tuesday afternoon about the affidavit. In a statement to CT Insider late Monday for a separate story, she said, "The detention of Mr. Morocho, moments after he helped his child board the school bus, shocks the conscience, and we will continue to vigorously pursue and protect his rights in Connecticut."

Morocho Arteaga entered the United States without inspection — a misdemeanor offense under federal law — and was released after encountering U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents during the administration of former President Joe Biden, according to DHS.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

According to the petition filed by Foden on Morocho Arteaga's behalf, an immigration judge in Hartford denied his application for asylum and ordered his removal from the United States in November 2024. Morocho Arteaga appealed the judge's ruling later that same month, the petition says. CT Insider confirmed that appeal is still pending.

The first of two videos taken from the school bus's cameras begins with a silver car pulling out of a nearby church’s parking lot and up to the intersection of Second Avenue and Rowan Street in front of the stopped bus. As it does, a handful of dark vehicles with flashing red-and-blue lights — consistent with other videos of ICE vehicles filmed in Danbury that week — box another car in on the opposite side of the nearby intersection.

The person in the silver car then gets out and holds up a phone, apparently filming.

The second video taken from the bus cameras shows the bus stop as a group of children who are lined up in the church parking lot, many of them wearing backpacks, as a group of adults stand nearby. As the children get on the bus, a silver car drives in front of it.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Moments later, after the last child is on the bus but before its doors are closed, the group of adults suddenly looks toward the intersection, then run away. A person then runs over from the area where the silver car pulled out, speaks with the bus driver, then walks back toward the intersection. The bus pulls into the church parking lot in order to shield the children from viewing the incident, the city’s superintendent of schools told CT Insider. Then the video ends.

CT Insider also reviewed other videos and a photo that have circulated among advocates in recent weeks. One shows four black vehicles with flashing red-and-blue lights surrounding a white or silver car. Agents in khaki protective vests and patches consistent with those worn by ICE officers in other videos taken in Danbury that week — some of them masked — surround the vehicles. Two are putting a man who appears to be handcuffed in the back of one of the black cars. The woman filming can be heard indicating the man being detained had recently dropped his child off at the bus stop.

Morocho Arteaga said in the new court filing that after the agents arrested him, one asked if he had a criminal record. When he said no, Morocho Arteaga said the agent told him that was good "because if I didn't have a criminal record, the office would release me in three hours."

Morocho Arteaga said in the affidavit the agents then placed him in hand and leg shackles and placed him in a van with 10 others and transported him to Hartford. Once there, an ICE agent spoke to all the detainees in Spanish, urging them to take "voluntary departure" — a process that allows an immigrant who is in the United States without permanent status to voluntarily leave the country rather than risk forcible deportation, the affidavit continues.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"The officer then asked each person if they wanted to sign," Morocho Arteaga said in the affidavit. "I said no. One couple said that they would accept, and they were taken to another side of the office."

Once the detainees were in a holding cell, Morocho Arteaga said the agents called them one-by-one for processing. When it was his turn, Morocho Arteaga said the agents told him to call someone to arrange for them to pick up the son he had dropped off at the bus stop that morning up from school. They also asked him about his 1-year-old, who is a U.S. citizen he said.

"The officer asked about the mother of my children, how far was her work from Danbury, but they did not ask about her (immigration) status," he said in the filing. "The question was focused on who would pick up my son from school."

Morocho Arteaga said an officer gave him a form that indicated he was being transferred to Colorado. Then, around 5 p.m., Morocho Arteaga said in the filing that agents handcuffed him again.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"The officers told us that we were going to Boston and then to Colorado," he said.

ICE released a list of five men Friday it said it had arrested as part of the four-day operation in Connecticut late last month. CT Insider confirmed ICE was holding at least three of the five at the Denver Contract Detention Facility, also called the Aurora ICE Processing Center, in Aurora, Colorado. CT Insider has also spoken to the families of two other men who were arrested during the operation and who have been held at the Aurora facility.

However, Morocho Arteaga said an officer then took off his handcuffs and sent him back to the holding cell. After a short wait, they told him to call his family to come pick him up. After that, Morocho Arteaga said agents took him to a different building where they fitted him with a GPS ankle monitor and told him he could not leave the state without asking permission.

authors: Capitol City Now, Hannah Meisel, Jerry Nowicki

text:
CHICAGO (CAPITOL NEWS ILLINOIS) — The state of Illinois and city of Chicago, along with a coalition of other states and cities controlled by Democrats, are suing the Trump administration to block a new federal rule that would give immigration officials broader authority to deny green cards to those who have legally been using public aid like Medicaid and food stamps.

The new rule, set to go into effect Friday, expands longstanding policy that bars immigrants from obtaining green cards if they are likely to become primarily dependent on the government. Historically, immigration officers have deemed green card applicants as potential “public charges” based on participation in cash assistance programs like welfare and use of government-funded long-term institutionalized care like in a nursing home.

But after Friday, that list will expand to more common uses of public aid by immigrant families including Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — commonly known as food stamps — and federal housing programs. While undocumented immigrants are already ineligible for public aid, mixed-status families can legally benefit from those programs via children who are U.S. citizens.

Additionally, most noncitizens without green cards are similarly ineligible for government assistance, but certain lawfully present noncitizens, including refugees, asylum seekers and human trafficking survivors, have been allowed to use these programs. However, the massive budget bill championed by President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans last summer significantly restricted eligibility to those groups.

The Democratic leaders behind the lawsuits, filed Monday in New York federal court, warned the rule will sow fear and confusion in immigrant families. A statement from Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office said the rule will put immigrants in a trick box as it defines “no clear limit on which benefits, or how much use, count against an applicant, leaving families to guess which forms of assistance might put their immigration status at risk.”

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson called the rule “cruel” and noted that more than half a million Chicago residents were born outside the U.S.

“Chicago will not stand by while the federal government forces immigrant families to choose between putting food on the table, taking their children to the doctor, or protecting their ability to remain in this country,” he said in a statement.

The lawsuits allege the rule usurps Congress and gives individual immigration officers too much power. The lawsuit filed by Illinois and 21 other states cites broad language in the new rule that authorizes immigration officers to consider “whether an alien has applied for, been approved or certified for, received, or will likely receive means-tested public benefits.”

“Congress never intended for the public charge ground to be weaponized against immigrants and their family members who merely use supplemental or temporary amounts of public assistance to which they are lawfully entitled,” the states’ lawsuit said. “Yet that is exactly what Defendants now seek to do through the final rule challenged here.”

The Democratic leaders also point to the rule’s explicit refusal to spell out how officers should weigh a green card applicant’s participation in a certain program and how long the benefits were used. By “not drawing distinctions” between supplemental and other benefits, the states’ lawsuit said, the new rule runs into the same legal problems that doomed the Trump administration’s first attempt at altering the public charge rule in 2019.

“Like the 2019 Rule, the 2026 Final Rule enables Defendants to make a noncitizen’s receipt of supplemental non-cash benefits, including a citizen child’s use of supplemental benefits to which they are statutorily entitled, however minimal or however long ago, indicative of being inadmissible as a ‘public charge,’” the states’ lawsuit said.

Courts blocked earlier Trump attempt

The 2019 effort was blocked by federal courts, including the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals, though the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately allowed the rule to take effect everywhere but Illinois in early 2020. However, the Biden administration halted the appeals and set its own public charge rules, which were substantially similar to 1999-era policies.

The Democratic leaders warned of a cascade effect caused by the new rule as noncitizens are prompted to disenroll from public benefits. Without Medicaid coverage, Raoul’s office warned, immigrants will delay care and turn to emergency rooms, “straining safety-net hospitals and community health centers, and increasing costs for everyone.”

Schools could also be at risk of losing automatic certification for free and reduced-price meal programs when SNAP and Medicaid enrollment drops below certain thresholds, which would impair access to school food programs for all children in that school. Falling enrollment in public aid would also shrink federal Title I education funding for schools in areas with higher immigrant populations.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security estimates federal Medicaid funding to states could see a $4 billion annual cut, while SNAP payments would shrink by $1 billion annually.

But a DHS spokesperson cited those cuts as a positive, accusing the states and cities challenging the law of being “terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs.”

“We’re shaking in our boots over this supposedly terrible outcome,” Chandler Rebel said in a statement.

text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — ICE is expanding its state and local law enforcement partnerships across Tennessee, strengthening cooperation to identify and remove criminal illegal aliens who pose public safety threats.

As of Sept. 9, ICE has 120 of these 287(g) partners in Tennessee. Participating agencies may operate under the Jail Enforcement, Warrant Service Officer and Task Force models. Across the country, ICE has signed 2,466 memoranda of agreement with 287(g) partners.

“287(g) is a critical public safety initiative that gives law enforcement agencies another tool to protect their communities,” said ICE Public Safety Partnership Division Assistant Director Russell Hott. “By working closely with sheriffs, chiefs and our state partners across Tennessee, law enforcement is able to apprehend criminal illegal aliens who continue to prey on and victimize local communities and remove those threats from our neighborhoods.”

The 287(g) program is an invaluable resource that provides state and local law enforcement agencies with another tool to enhance public safety in their communities by arresting and removing criminal illegal aliens involved in gang activity, violent crimes, sex offenses, drug trafficking and numerous other forms of illicit activity. Since Jan. 20, 2025, ICE enforcement activity in the state has included more than 1,300 arrests by 287(g) partners and 542 encounters with aliens in local custody.

Last month, the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office became an operational 287(g) partner and arrested Reniery Garcia-Godoy, a criminal illegal alien from Honduras, on the first day of the partnership. Garcia-Godoy, who was taken into custody near the Tennessee-Alabama state line, had two felony convictions for sexual battery in Franklin, Tennessee, and has since been removed from the U.S.

These criminal illegal aliens remain in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.

“Partnerships like these are essential to public safety,” said ERO New Orleans acting Field Office Director Scott Ladwig. “The continued expansion of 287(g) in Tennessee demonstrates the commitment of ICE and our law enforcement partners to remove dangerous criminal aliens from our communities.”

ERO New Orleans officials and ICE’s Public Safety Partnership Division recently attended the Tennessee Sheriffs’ Association Conference to meet with sheriffs and other law enforcement leaders about the program. Earlier this year, Tennessee passed a law requiring all sheriffs’ offices to enter into a 287(g) agreement by Jan. 1, 2027. Agencies that do not comply could lose certain state funding.

Seven out of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. For more information about the 287(g) program, visit ICE.gov.

Human rights seize the discussion about AI and pull it away from machines and towards the human.

text:
The Hugging Face hack and the subsequent string of frontier AI lab researchers raising the alarm about existential risk has launched AI’s dangers back into the headlines.

Whilst these hype and doom narratives are baffling to anyone not deep in Silicon Valley’s international networks, these risks deserve our attention and scrutiny. Where they prove dangerous and imminent, like in cyber security, the Government should act. However, we cannot let the panic about future harms divert our attention from the harms that have already arrived.

You fall in love and you decide to get married, but your application for a marriage licence is rejected because your partner is Greek and a DWP algorithm flagged you as a potential scammer.1 You study in the library every weekend for a year, determined to make your A-Level grades to get into your dream university, but because no one in your school had ever gotten an A* before, an algorithm pulled you down and you missed your offer.2 You are pulled out of your home in the middle of the night for a committing a crime in a city you’ve never been to because a biased algorithm matched your face incorrectly.3 These are all examples of the life-changing impacts of government AI systems already going wrong.

Liberty has been watching as AI has become the plaster to stick on many of the Government’s problems. With ailing public services and little money to fix them, AI and automation offer shiny solutions that seem to answer to successive governments’ complaints about the state (too slow with too much bureaucracy). Starmer hailed AI as the ‘defining opportunity of our generation’4 and a development with ‘revolutionary’ potential.5 However, amidst the excitement, the Government has consistently undervalued the risks that ill-thought-out AI adoption automates into our state.

We are particularly concerned about the accelerating use of AI in policing and criminal justice. We have already seen police officers using AI systems to try to influence criminal justice outcomes.6 Even routine uses of AI like redaction, transcription, and report drafting can raise issues of bias and accuracy, with potentially serious consequences for the evidence chain. Higher risk systems like facial recognition and predictive policing are already impacting people’s lives: Alvi Choudhury was arrested after facial recognition incorrectly matched him to a suspect in a city he had never been to.7 If the Government continues to roll out AI without proper safeguards, more people will be misidentified or flagged by racially biased algorithms, and more people will have their access to public services and their criminal justice outcomes shaped by AI scores they never see or understand.

The UK has long been the one of most surveilled democracies in the world. However, police forces and intelligence agencies have lacked the manpower to use all their camera networks and data to their full extent. Now, with AI systems able to scrape these massive data sources and make them useful, it will hand huge power to governments. We need only look to the US to see how this can be used to target migrants, activists, and journalists.

It is tempting, in the face of technological innovation and a hype cycle driven by those innovators, to think of this moment as unprecedented. Of course, AI creates new, unique challenges for tech companies, policymakers, and for society. But this is not the first time we have grappled with a new technology.

Human rights frameworks emerged out of the destruction wrought by a technological revolution. Railways, census data, communication systems, the administrative processes of the factory – the machinery of the modern, industrialised state – gave Hitler’s genocidal regime unprecedented power over its people. Whilst the concepts that underpinned human rights frameworks had been developing for centuries, it was in the wake of the Holocaust that they were adopted and codified en masse and the world agreed: ‘All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.’8 The scale of the war’s destruction crystallised the importance of each human life, and the rights that make a life worth living.

Technological innovation is once again increasing state (and non-state) actors’ power over our lives. We should not wait for tragedy to act to constrain this power again, and human rights is the toolkit we built to do so. Human rights also provide something that AI safety, transparency, and ethics cannot: a universal set of values and principles that we have collectively agreed are important. They are globally salient; 80% of UN member states have ratified four or more of the core international human rights treaties.9 This global recognition makes human rights the best foundation for aligning AI with values that resonate across cultures.

Human rights seize the discussion about AI and pull it away from machines and towards the human. They are a way of inserting humanity and our needs back into these systems and re-asserting what is useful and important to our lives. It is not inevitable that innovation should erode our freedoms and our dignity.

As Burnham begins his first Parliament as Prime Minister, he should take the opportunity to turn a new leaf and reset the Government’s approach to AI. The Labour Government must take a human first approach to technology policy. Putting human rights at the heart of his approach would be the first step towards building better tech for all Britons.

1 Kiran Stacey, ‘UK officials use AI to decide on issues from benefits to marriage licenses’, Guardian, 23 October 2023.

2 Pamela Duncan, Niamh McIntyre, Rhi Storer and Cath Levett, ‘Who won and who lost: when A-levels meet the algorithm’, Guardian, 13 August 2020.

3 Robert Booth and Mark Wilding, ‘Facial recognition error prompts police to arrest Asian man for burglary 100 miles away’, Guardian, 25 February 2026.

4 Rt Hon Sir Keir Starmer MP, ‘PM speech on AI Opportunities Action Plan’, Prime Minister’s Office, 10 Downing Street, 13 January 2025.

5 Ibid.

6 Rebecca Sherdley, ‘Senior detective under investigation over use of AI’, BBC News, 10 August 2026.

7 Robert Booth and Mark Wilding, ‘Facial recognition error prompts police to arrest Asian man for burglary 100 miles away’, Guardian, 25 February 2026.

8 Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 1

9 UN Treaty Body Database, United Nations Human Rights Treaty Bodies website, accessed 02/09/26.

Rochester, N.Y. — A federal judge has decided a Rochester man who sent an email to the Department of Homeland Security had his First Amendment rights violated.

David Streever sent an email to Todd Lyons, then the acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, criticizing the conduct of federal agents after the shooting deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis. The email compared Lyons to a former Nazi official.

BACKGROUND: Rochester man warned by ICE after writing blistering letter to agency, attorney says | Rochester man sues ICE on free speech grounds over critical email sent to its former head

Streever filed a lawsuit claiming special agents visited his home in June and presented his wife with a warning notice, informing him that the email he sent months earlier was considered a threat. Streever was on a trip to Finland at the time.

In a ruling dated Tuesday, U.S. District Court Judge Rudolph Contreras wrote in part, "Mr. Streever has a right to express his political views through non-threatening speech, however degrading the speech might be."

Contreras also said DHS likely infringed on Streever's First Amendment rights by threatening to prosecute him if he didn't stop his criticism.

In July, a Homeland Security spokesperson told 13WHAM it does not comment on ongoing investigations and added, "Any allegation DHS and its components are attempting to 'squash' free speech is categorically FALSE. Anyone who assaults or threatens our law enforcement officers will face the consequences."

text:
Commercial-driver safety has become part of a growing national debate following fatal crashes that raised questions about licensing, driver training and English-language proficiency requirements. Federal officials have responded with increased scrutiny of immigrant commercial drivers and state licensing practices. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security recently posted an AI-generated image depicting a bearded South Asian man identified as “Mr. Singh” facing a character resembling Optimus Prime with a DHS insignia. The image included the message “Get off our roads; you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” The post drew criticism from Sikh and Indian American organizations that said it unfairly associated an entire community with dangerous driving and immigration violations. DHS later removed the post. State Rep. Mark Tisdel released the following statement:

“The DHS post was wrong. The Sikh community has an extraordinary record of success, entrepreneurship, service and contribution in this country. These are our neighbors, business owners, professionals, workers and community leaders. To single them out and suggest that an entire community should somehow be viewed with suspicion is not only offensive, it is the epitome of ignorance and a waste of government time and resources.

“There are legitimate safety standards that apply to commercial drivers, and those standards should be enforced fairly and consistently for everyone. But a broader challenge should never be reduced to a stereotype about one community. If there are gaps in language proficiency, literacy, education or training, then we should address those problems directly and help people meet the standard.

“Government should be solving problems, not creating scapegoats.”

title: 'Alligator Alcatraz' detainees were held in cages the size of a phone booth
description:

Asked about the inspector general’s findings at a news conference Monday, DeSantis said he hadn’t read the report but defended Florida’s unprecedented work to carry out federal immigration enforcement.
At the time, federal officials said detainees were transferred out of “Alligator Alcatraz” because of hurricane-season safety concerns.

text:
This story was originally published by The Florida Trib.

When federal investigators showed up unannounced at the sprawling pop-up prison in the Florida Everglades in January, they found something they had never seen at any other immigration detention center in the country: Detainees at “Alligator Alcatraz” were being held for up to nearly two hours in small metal cages roughly the size of a phone booth.

The practice at the now-shuttered facility is “unprecedented,” presents “significant risks to detainee health and safety,” and “does not align with standards for humane treatment,” according to a recently released 33-page report by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General, which detailed a litany of failures at the state-built facility to comply with standards for medical care, personal hygiene, environmental safety and food service.

According to the report, between July 17, 2025, and Jan. 18, 2026, the facility confined 79 detainees in the small metal enclosures for periods of time ranging from several minutes to just shy of two hours, “a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities,” the report reads. The floor of the cages measured roughly 4 feet 3 inches by 4 feet 3 inches, and they stood 7 feet 9 inches tall, according to the report.

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report continues, adding that inspectors observed “locking mechanisms” on the cages.

The report gives a rare glimpse into the sprawling makeshift facility that was built in a matter of days by Gov. Ron DeSantis’ administration. From the start, human rights watchdogs and those held inside sounded the alarm about a facility they said imprisoned detainees without any charges, violated their constitutional rights, and subjected them to inhumane and unsanitary conditions. Democratic state lawmakers and outside observers were barred from inspecting the compound, which, along with another state-run immigration detention center, carries an estimated $1 billion price tag. And yet the hastily built facility and the DeSantis administration officials behind it have largely avoided oversight and accountability from Florida’s Republican-dominated state Legislature, where lawmakers last week signed off on another $250 million funding request for the state agency that built the compound.

Asked about the inspector general’s findings at a news conference Monday, DeSantis said he hadn’t read the report but defended Florida’s unprecedented work to carry out federal immigration enforcement.

“No one’s stepped up to the level we have,” DeSantis said.

“And the fact that we represent 6.5-7% of the U.S. population and yet we account for between 40% and 50% of all state and local immigration arrests, you know, that should tell you that we’re really doing it right,” he added.

Doubling down on an approach that made “Alligator Alcatraz” a national symbol of the state’s aggressive immigration crackdown, a spokesperson for DeSantis told the Miami Herald that the administration would make the metal cages “even smaller” if they could.

Amnesty International had previously detailed allegations that detainees were being confined for hours in a small metal cage known as “the box” as punishment, treatment that the human rights organization said “amounts to torture.”

Meanwhile, attorneys for environmental organizations that filed suit against the facility said the findings of the inspector general’s report show the compound was not only “damaging to the Everglades” but also “cruel beyond measure.”

“The report reveals the depraved disregard for life that drove enormous human suffering and extensive environmental destruction in the Everglades,” said Elise Bennett, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Trump and DeSantis’s obsession with spectacle and cruelty has hurt people, irreplaceable natural treasures and Floridians, who’ll be footing the bill for this monstrosity for years to come.”

Nearly two hours in a metal cage

The findings of the inspector general’s report aligned with many of the concerns raised by detainees, their families and their attorneys since the earliest days of the facility.

Inspectors found detainees held in cramped housing units ringed by chain-link fencing that limited them to 28 square feet per detainee, “well below the required minimum.” At the time of the inspection, detainees in certain housing units had no access to a law library or legal materials, and telephones installed shortly before the inspection were inoperable, leaving detainees without the ability to call their attorneys or ICE case workers.

Inspectors documented showers infested with bugs, interviewed detainees who said they “did not have access to clean drinking water,” and found that medical providers onsite were not properly documenting the conditions of detainees experiencing withdrawal from drugs or alcohol, raising questions about their access to adequate medical care. (Symptoms of withdrawal can range from mild discomfort to severe seizures, and complications can be deadly.)

Detainees were limited to three showers a week, and just one hour of recreation time three days a week – far less than standards stipulate, the inspectors found. Additionally, some freezers at the site were operating above the recommended temperature, increasing the risk of foodborne illnesses for detainees and staff alike.

The report’s most stunning finding was the “unprecedented” use of the phone booth-sized cages, which facility staff described as “calming areas.”

Over the course of six months, nearly 80 detainees were held in the enclosures for an average of 59 minutes, with the shortest confinement lasting just under seven minutes and the longest stretching to one hour, 59 minutes and 18 seconds, just shy of the two-hour limit outlined in a facility policy.

Federal inspectors were not able to confirm reports that detainees in the enclosures were at times subjected to direct sunlight, high temperatures, and denial of food or water.

Still, the report noted that “[c]onfining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and well-being.”

Who’s in charge?

Even DHS’ Inspector General couldn’t quite get to the bottom of one of the most fundamental questions around the facility: who was actually in charge?

Federal officials maintained that DHS did not have any formal contract with the state of Florida to run the site, the report states, and ICE documents that list the “contractually obligated standards for each detention facility showed ‘N/A’,” for the South Florida facility.

When federal inspectors questioned the facility’s leadership and staff – who were employed by a private contractor – they couldn’t get a consistent answer as to which detention standards the facility was operating under, which “increases the risk that detainees may not receive appropriate care,” the report reads.

“[O]ne official stated it was ‘so gray as to whose place this is … and which standards to follow’,” the report continues.

Florida officials announced plans to close the facility in June, declaring the site had served its purpose – as federal court challenges dragged on and the costs of running the remote facility ballooned. At the time, federal officials said detainees were transferred out of “Alligator Alcatraz” because of hurricane-season safety concerns. ICE did not disclose how many detainees were moved or where they were taken.

While the DeSantis administration has shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz,” the DHS inspector general’s report notes that the findings regarding the immigration detention center “remain consequential.”

Florida is still operating yet another state-run immigration detention facility dubbed “Deportation Depot,” which as of Aug. 27, 2026, held 1,028 detainees, according to the report. Federal documents detailing contractually obligated detention standards for that facility state simply “N/A,” like the Everglades facility before it.

Kate Payne is The Florida Trib’s state government reporter. She can be reached at kate.payne@floridatrib.org

What They're Saying McClintock argued that sanctuary policies interfere with federal immigration enforcement and create public-safety risks.
Supporters of sanctuary policies also argue that limiting local participation in immigration enforcement can encourage immigrants to report crimes and cooperate with police.
Litigation over state and local immigration policies is also continuing.
text:
The Justice Department sued Hoboken, Jersey City, Newark and Paterson, New Jersey, in May 2025, challenging municipal policies restricting local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. A federal judge dismissed the case without prejudice on June 24, finding that the federal government had not established standing because New Jersey's statewide Immigrant Trust Directive independently imposed many of the same restrictions. The ruling did not decide the legality of the cities' policies on the merits.

The debate also includes H.R. 7640, the Shut Down Sanctuary Policies Act, introduced by Subcommittee Chair Tom McClintock (R-CA) on Feb. 23. The legislation would establish federal requirements for state and local cooperation with immigration enforcement, restrict certain federal law enforcement grants to jurisdictions deemed noncompliant and create a private right of action in specified circumstances involving crimes committed after a jurisdiction declined to honor an immigration detainer.

The House Judiciary Committee approved H.R. 7640, as amended, by a 22-11 vote on March 5. The committee formally reported the legislation on March 12.

The Congressional Research Service identified 13 states and 225 localities as having sanctuary policies as of January 2025, citing a count by the Center for Immigration Studies. CRS cautioned that there is no agreed-upon legal definition of a sanctuary jurisdiction and that any count is imprecise because jurisdictions regularly change their policies.

What They're Saying

McClintock argued that sanctuary policies interfere with federal immigration enforcement and create public-safety risks. He cited the Shut Down Sanctuary Policies Act as a legislative response, saying the measure would preempt certain restrictions on cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, protect officers cooperating with federal authorities, redirect specified federal law enforcement grants and create a private right of action in certain cases.

Ranking Member Pramila Jayapal (D-WA) argued that requiring state and local law enforcement agencies to participate in federal immigration enforcement diverts resources from local public-safety responsibilities and can make immigrant communities less willing to cooperate with police. She also criticized the Trump administration's broader immigration-enforcement campaign.

David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, testified that restrictions on local participation in immigration enforcement do not increase crime. His written testimony cited 12 studies that he said found no increase in crime associated with limits on local participation in immigration enforcement. Bier also argued that Congress should require the Department of Homeland Security to focus enforcement resources on people who pose public-safety threats.

Jeffrey Gahler, sheriff of Harford County, Maryland, argued that Maryland's Community Trust Act restricts cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities and could require jails to release people sought by ICE. Gahler is the lead plaintiff among 17 Maryland sheriffs challenging the law in federal court.

The other witnesses were Patricia Fox, whose daughter Carissa "Luu" Aspnes was permanently disabled after a hit-and-run crash in Colorado involving an undocumented Venezuelan immigrant, and Marcus Coleman, whose daughter Dalilah was permanently disabled after a multivehicle crash involving an undocumented immigrant.

Political Stakes

The hearing highlighted competing views over the relationship between federal immigration enforcement and state and local policing. Republicans on the subcommittee argued that jurisdictions should cooperate with ICE detainers and information requests and pointed to crimes involving undocumented immigrants as evidence of the risks they associate with sanctuary policies.

Jayapal and other Democrats argued that local law enforcement resources should remain focused on criminal enforcement rather than federal civil immigration enforcement. Supporters of sanctuary policies also argue that limiting local participation in immigration enforcement can encourage immigrants to report crimes and cooperate with police.

CRS has noted that jurisdictions adopt such policies for different reasons, including concerns about legal liability from immigration detainers, limited local resources, family separation and removals of immigrants with minor or no criminal records.

The Justice Department has separately opened a civil rights investigation into whether Fairfax County, Virginia, Commonwealth's Attorney Steve Descano's office discriminated against U.S. citizens through its plea bargaining, charging and sentencing policies involving undocumented defendants. The department said on May 6 that it had reached no conclusions about the allegations.

The relationship between sanctuary policies and crime remains disputed. Bier cited academic research that he said does not show increased crime from policies limiting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, while Gahler and Republican members emphasized individual cases in which undocumented immigrants were accused or convicted of crimes after interactions with local authorities.

The term "sanctuary jurisdiction" itself also has no uniform legal definition. CRS notes that jurisdictions differ significantly in how they restrict cooperation with ICE, including policies governing information sharing, immigration detainers and participation in federal immigration-enforcement programs.

Those distinctions complicate comparisons among jurisdictions and broad claims about the effects of sanctuary policies nationwide.

The Bottom Line

H.R. 7640 has been reported by the House Judiciary Committee and placed on the Union Calendar but has not received a House floor vote.

Litigation over state and local immigration policies is also continuing. Gahler and 16 other Maryland sheriffs are challenging Maryland's Community Trust Act, while the Justice Department has filed a separate federal lawsuit challenging the same law.

The hearing record also remained open for members to submit additional materials following the Sept. 1 proceeding.

title: Illinois, Chicago sue to block Trump plan to restrict green cards to legal Medicaid, SNAP users
description:
However, the massive budget bill championed by President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans last summer significantly restricted eligibility to those groups.
260506-JOHNSON-JN-0414.JPG The lawsuits allege the rule usurps Congress and gives individual immigration officers too much power.
The Democratic leaders warned of a cascade effect caused by the new rule as noncitizens are prompted to disenroll from public benefits.
Falling enrollment in public aid would also shrink federal Title I education funding for schools in areas with higher immigrant populations.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security estimates federal Medicaid funding to states could see a $4 billion annual cut, while SNAP payments would shrink by $1 billion annually.
text:
CHICAGO — The state of Illinois and city of Chicago, along with a coalition of other states and cities controlled by Democrats, are suing the Trump administration to block a new federal rule that would give immigration officials broader authority to deny green cards to those who have legally been using public aid like Medicaid and food stamps.

The new rule, set to go into effect Friday, expands longstanding policy that bars immigrants from obtaining green cards if they are likely to become primarily dependent on the government. Historically, immigration officers have deemed green card applicants as potential “public charges” based on participation in cash assistance programs like welfare and use of government-funded long-term institutionalized care like in a nursing home.

But after Friday, that list will expand to more common uses of public aid by immigrant families including Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — commonly known as food stamps — and federal housing programs. While undocumented immigrants are already ineligible for public aid, mixed-status families can legally benefit from those programs via children who are U.S. citizens.

Additionally, most noncitizens without green cards are similarly ineligible for government assistance, but certain lawfully present noncitizens, including refugees, asylum seekers and human trafficking survivors, have been allowed to use these programs. However, the massive budget bill championed by President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans last summer significantly restricted eligibility to those groups.

The Democratic leaders behind the lawsuits, filed Monday in New York federal court, warned the rule will sow fear and confusion in immigrant families. A statement from Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office said the rule will put immigrants in a trick box as it defines “no clear limit on which benefits, or how much use, count against an applicant, leaving families to guess which forms of assistance might put their immigration status at risk.”

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson called the rule “cruel” and noted that more than half a million Chicago residents were born outside the U.S.

“Chicago will not stand by while the federal government forces immigrant families to choose between putting food on the table, taking their children to the doctor, or protecting their ability to remain in this country,” he said in a statement.

260506-JOHNSON-JN-0414.JPG

The lawsuits allege the rule usurps Congress and gives individual immigration officers too much power. The lawsuit filed by Illinois and 21 other states cites broad language in the new rule that authorizes immigration officers to consider “whether an alien has applied for, been approved or certified for, received, or will likely receive means-tested public benefits.”

“Congress never intended for the public charge ground to be weaponized against immigrants and their family members who merely use supplemental or temporary amounts of public assistance to which they are lawfully entitled,” the states’ lawsuit said. “Yet that is exactly what Defendants now seek to do through the final rule challenged here.”

The Democratic leaders also point to the rule’s explicit refusal to spell out how officers should weigh a green card applicant’s participation in a certain program and how long the benefits were used. By “not drawing distinctions” between supplemental and other benefits, the states’ lawsuit said, the new rule runs into the same legal problems that doomed the Trump administration’s first attempt at altering the public charge rule in 2019.

“Like the 2019 Rule, the 2026 Final Rule enables Defendants to make a noncitizen’s receipt of supplemental non-cash benefits, including a citizen child’s use of supplemental benefits to which they are statutorily entitled, however minimal or however long ago, indicative of being inadmissible as a ‘public charge,’” the states’ lawsuit said.

Courts blocked earlier Trump attempt

The 2019 effort was blocked by federal courts, including the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals, though the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately allowed the rule to take effect everywhere but Illinois in early 2020. However, the Biden administration halted the appeals and set its own public charge rules, which were substantially similar to 1999-era policies.

The Democratic leaders warned of a cascade effect caused by the new rule as noncitizens are prompted to disenroll from public benefits. Without Medicaid coverage, Raoul’s office warned, immigrants will delay care and turn to emergency rooms, “straining safety-net hospitals and community health centers, and increasing costs for everyone.”

Schools could also be at risk of losing automatic certification for free and reduced-price meal programs when SNAP and Medicaid enrollment drops below certain thresholds, which would impair access to school food programs for all children in that school. Falling enrollment in public aid would also shrink federal Title I education funding for schools in areas with higher immigrant populations.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security estimates federal Medicaid funding to states could see a $4 billion annual cut, while SNAP payments would shrink by $1 billion annually.

But a DHS spokesperson cited those cuts as a positive, accusing the states and cities challenging the law of being “terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs.”

“We’re shaking in our boots over this supposedly terrible outcome,” Chandler Rebel said in a statement.

description:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) may no longer issue a “warning notice” – threatening prosecution against a US citizen – for criticizing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal judge in Washington DC ruled on Tuesday.
Contreras ruled the notice “practically shouts that Mr Streever may be prosecuted if he continues to engage in his political speech”.
A DHS spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian: “Any allegation DHS and its components are attempting to ‘squash’ free speech is categorically FALSE.
Immigration enforcement officials have consistently justified federal agents’ aggressive actions by claiming they are protecting immigration enforcement officers.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) may no longer issue a “warning notice” – threatening prosecution against a US citizen – for criticizing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal judge in Washington DC ruled on Tuesday.

Judge Rudolph Contreras sided with David Streever, a New York man who accused DHS officials of violating his first amendment rights when they showed up first at his home in June with a “warning notice”, claiming he made a threat against former ICE director Todd Lyons, and then to a hotel where Streever and his young daughter were staying.

The notice and visits were in response to an email Streever sent Lyons in January, after federal agents fatally shot two US citizens amid an immigration crackdown in Minnesota. In the email, Streever called Lyons a “monstrous human being”, compared him to Nazi and warned him that his own conscience would “eat himself alive”.

Contreras ruled the notice “practically shouts that Mr Streever may be prosecuted if he continues to engage in his political speech”.

“Americans have long voiced their displeasure with their government. The Declaration of Independence itself is a list of grievances between Americans and the British government. And Americans have not always indulged in the elevated prose of the declaration. Government officials have long endured ‘vehement, caustic and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks.’ Today is no different,” Contreras wrote.

The court order is limited in that it prohibits the DHS, its secretary, Markwayne Mullin, or ICE from issuing another “warning notice”, making similar threats or pursuing prosecution for his speech while Streever’s case continues in court.

A DHS spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian: “Any allegation DHS and its components are attempting to ‘squash’ free speech is categorically FALSE. ICE investigates all credible threats towards its employees and officers, including threats to the ICE Director.”

DHS law enforcement officers are “experiencing coordinated campaigns of violence against them,” including large increases in assaults, vehicular attacks and death threats, the spokesperson said.

“Anyone who assaults or threatens our law enforcement officers will face the consequences,” they added.

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (Fire), a non-profit first amendment advocacy group, represented Streever in his lawsuit.

“I’m deeply relieved that the court affirmed what I knew all along: that I am permitted to speak my conscience in the United States of America, including when I criticize government officials,” Streever said in a statement.

Streever added: “While I wish this ordeal hadn’t happened, hopefully this incident will serve as a reminder that the first amendment protects us all.”

The DHS previously defended its investigation into Streever by tying his email into a larger trend of threats made against law enforcement officials – particularly those enforcing the Trump administration’s anti-immigration agenda.

Immigration enforcement officials have consistently justified federal agents’ aggressive actions by claiming they are protecting immigration enforcement officers.

Contreras said his ruling allows DHS officials to investigate future conduct to ensure the safety of law enforcement and public officials, so long as it does not infringe on Streever’s protected speech.

text:
Democrats are ahead of Republicans on some of the issues most important to voters —immigration, health care and the economy—according to a new poll.

In the New York Times/Siena University poll, 51 percent of likely voter respondents said they trusted Democrats to excel in their work on the economy over Republicans, while 45 percent said the same of Republicans in comparison to Democrats and 4 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

When it came to the topic of immigration, 52 percent of respondents backed Democrats’ performance over Republicans, while 45 percent backed Republicans over Democrats and 3 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

And when it came to health care, 60 percent of respondents backed Democrats’ performance over Republicans, while 36 percent backed Republicans over Democrats and 5 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

The Times/Siena poll spells trouble for Republicans as the midterms elections are only a few weeks out. The party is already dealing with issues like President Trump’s slumping approval rating, the unpopular war in Iran that is nearing its seventh month and Democrats recently excelling on the generic congressional ballot.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.5 percent as of late Tuesday afternoon, while his disapproval rating was at 58.2 percent.

However, a top political adviser to Trump recently said he was “cautiously optimistic” that Republicans can hold onto Congress.

“I won’t predict, you know, how many seats are going to be in either chamber come November,” James Blair told NBC News’s podcast, “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition.” “But, I do think there is a path for us to retain both majorities and defy history.”

The Times/Siena poll took place between Sept. 8 and 13, featuring 1,503 likely voters and a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

title: 'I feel kidnapped': Latino immigrants say they're in legal limbo after being deported to country in Africa
authors: Laura Romero, Matt Rivers, ABC News

text:
Since last month, Yasmany Moreno de Armas has been living what he calls a "nightmare." The 32-year-old Cuban's new home is in the Central African Republic, a country currently classified as an extreme-risk destination for Americans due to armed conflict, violent crime and the threat of terrorism.

Ten years ago, Moreno de Armas arrived in the U.S. after fleeing Cuba. He was legally allowed into the country under a policy that permitted Cubans who reached U.S. soil to stay and pursue legal residency.

Moreno de Armas was living in Miami with his family and working at a meatpacking plant when federal immigration authorities detained him last May. He had been trying to obtain legal status through asylum after other forms of legal relief were denied.

He was placed in federal custody and moved among detention centers across the country. Last May, while in a detention facility in Louisiana, he told ABC News he believed he was being moved again when he was placed on a plane with a handful of other detainees.

Two hours into the flight, Moreno de Armas said he was told he was on a deportation flight to a country in Africa.

"I thought it was a lie," he said in Spanish.

Moreno de Armas is one of roughly 25,000 people deported to so-called third countries during the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown, according to the immigrant rights organization Human Rights First. Third-country deportations are the removal of immigrants to a foreign country where they do not hold citizenship or have personal ties.

The Immigration and Nationality Act allows the Department of Homeland Security to deport migrants to third countries when they have proven that they could be persecuted in their country of origin or if that country cannot receive them.

According to immigration lawyers and advocates, third-country removals are not new, but they are rare. In recent months, the Trump administration has ramped up third-country deportations after creating a web of formal deals with nearly three dozen countries to deport asylum seekers, refugees and migrants with criminal records with little to no warning.

Some of the new destinations include Liberia, Ghana, the Central African Republic and Sierra Leone.

"The Trump administration is systematically and very cruelly sending people to third countries without prior notice, without due process, without any opportunity to object to what is happening to them," immigration attorney Meredyth Yoon told ABC News.

"The administration is doing this in ways that are both extremely opaque and lacking transparency," she said.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said Moreno de Armas and other men ABC News interviewed "were deported to a safe country."

"We are applying the law as written," the agency said.

Moreno de Armas and the group of Latin American men deported to the Central African Republic told ABC News they were dismayed that the U.S. government warns its own citizens against traveling to that country. The U.S. State Department's travel advisory warns Americans not to travel there due to risks of unrest, crime, kidnapping, landmines, health issues and terrorism.

"This is a country that has been at war for 50 years, where the United States does not allow its American citizens to enter," Moreno de Armas said. "And every day we are at risk."

The men told ABC News they are in "legal limbo," alleging they were deported without their passports or identification documents.

"We don't have a visa here or any papers, we are illegal," said Aristides Fernandez Garcia, a Cuban immigrant who was also deported. "We're prisoners here, they won't let us leave or go anywhere. Right now, even if I want to and have the means to travel to any other country, I can't."

The International Organization for Migration, an organization within the United Nations, said it is providing assistance to individuals deported to the Central African Republic who choose to remain there, including food, health care and counseling on the options available to them.

Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said the U.S. has spent nearly $50 million on third-country deportation deals.

"I think the fact that the Trump administration is sending refugees to the most dangerous countries in the world, to countries run by corrupt autocrats where they've been arbitrarily detained and sent back to persecution and torture, shows that the administration has a complete disregard for due process, for international law and for human dignity," Arvey said.

"I feel kidnapped," Fernandez Garcia said. "They have violated all the rights that exist in life, because we are human beings."

text:
Quick Hits

TPS protection for El Salvador was previously scheduled to end on September 9, 2026, but USCIS has not announced a formal extension, termination, or blanket EAD auto-extension date beyond the current alert.

Salvadoran individuals present in the United States retain their TPS protection, including work authorization, pending a further announcement.

On January 17, 2025, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a Federal Register notice extending El Salvador’s TPS designation for eighteen months, from March 10, 2025, through September 9, 2026. The notice allowed eligible existing Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries to retain TPS through September 9, 2026, if they continued to meet eligibility requirements, and established a re-registration period from January 17 through March 18, 2025. DHS stated that USCIS would issue new employment authorization documents (EADs) with a September 9, 2026, expiration date to eligible beneficiaries who timely re-registered and applied for employment authorization.

USCIS also issued employer-facing guidance for certain Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries whose TPS-based EAD renewal applications remained pending. Qualifying employees could receive a USCIS notice extending an expired TPS-based EAD through September 9, 2026, and could present that notice with the expired EAD as List A documentation for Form I-9 purposes. USCIS instructed employers to use September 9, 2026, as the employment authorization expiration date for Form I-9 and E-Verify purposes.

USCIS’s current alert states that Salvadoran individuals present in the United States under TPS retain protection, including work authorization, pending a further announcement. Substantive updates are expected to be published on the USCIS El Salvador TPS webpage and the USCIS I-9 Central webpage for Form I-9 Related news.

Ogletree Deakins’ Immigration Practice Group will continue to monitor developments and will post updates on the Immigration blog as additional information becomes available.

title: Federal Court Temporarily Blocks DHS “Duration of Status” Rule | Seyfarth Shaw LLP
authors: Belma Burkic, Mia Batista, Dawn M. Lurie
description:
A federal district court in Massachusetts has temporarily postponed the effective date of a DHS rule that would have replaced the longstanding “duration of status” (D/S) admission framework for F, J, and I nonimmigrants with fixed periods of admission.
The rule was scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, but the court issued a preliminary injunction preventing DHS from implementing it while litigation continues.
For now, employers and F-1 employees may continue to rely on the existing D/S and practical training framework.
Under the proposed rule, USCIS sought to replace the long-standing Duration of Status (D/S) framework with fixed periods of admission.
The court also determined that DHS did not sufficiently evaluate the rule's significant economic and practical impacts on affected stakeholders.
text:
A federal district court in Massachusetts has temporarily postponed the effective date of a DHS rule that would have replaced the longstanding “duration of status” (D/S) admission framework for F, J, and I nonimmigrants with fixed periods of admission. The rule was scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, but the court issued a preliminary injunction preventing DHS from implementing it while litigation continues.

As a result, F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, I media representatives, and their dependents will continue to be admitted for duration of status for the time being, rather than receiving fixed admission periods that could require extension filings to remain in the United States.

For employers, the injunction also avoids, at least for now, significant new operational and tracking challenges under the fixed-period framework, particularly for employees working pursuant to CPT, OPT, and STEM OPT. The rule would have introduced additional extension-of-stay requirements and potentially separate timelines for maintaining F-1 status and employment authorization, requiring closer coordination among employees, schools, immigration counsel, and HR and creating additional risks of gaps or interruptions in employment authorization. For now, employers and F-1 employees may continue to rely on the existing D/S and practical training framework.

The court’s order pauses implementation of the rule but does not permanently invalidate it. The federal government is expected to appeal the decision, and further developments are likely in the coming weeks.

Background:

By way of background, the United States has historically admitted individuals in F, J, and I status for the duration of their approved academic program, exchange program, or media assignment, rather than for a fixed period. This framework, commonly referred to as Duration of Status (D/S), has allowed these individuals to remain in the United States as long as needed to complete their authorized activities without periodic extension filings.

Under the proposed rule, USCIS sought to replace the long-standing Duration of Status (D/S) framework with fixed periods of admission. As a result, F, J, and I nonimmigrants requiring additional time to complete their studies, exchange programs, employment, or assignments would generally have been required to file an extension of stay application with USCIS or obtain a new visa abroad. In addition, the proposed rule would have restricted academic mobility, shortened certain grace periods, expanded the circumstances under which unlawful presence could accrue, and narrowed eligibility for I nonimmigrant status by imposing stricter requirements on qualifying foreign media organizations and their representatives. These changes, among others, would have represented a significant departure from the existing system and would have imposed substantial new compliance, tracking, and filing obligations on foreign nationals, educational institutions, exchange program sponsors, media organizations, and employers.

The rule was originally scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, and included transition provisions for individuals currently in F, J, or I status.

On August 18, 2026, a coalition of labor unions and higher education organizations filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts challenging the rule. On September 14, 2026, the court issued a preliminary injunction prohibiting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from implementing or enforcing the rule pending further order of the court.

Court’s Findings:

In granting the preliminary injunction, U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV concluded that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims that the Final Rule violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Specifically, the court found that DHS failed to adequately demonstrate how the rule would meaningfully advance its stated objectives, including enhancing national security, reducing fraud, and preventing overstays. The court also determined that DHS did not sufficiently evaluate the rule's significant economic and practical impacts on affected stakeholders.

Additionally, the court found that DHS failed to adequately address the nearly 22,000 public comments submitted during the rulemaking process and did not meaningfully consider less restrictive alternatives proposed by stakeholders. Based on these findings, the court granted nationwide preliminary relief, preventing the rule from taking effect unless and until further judicial action permits its implementation.

Final Thoughts

Although the court's preliminary injunction has temporarily halted implementation of the rule, the litigation remains ongoing and the rule could still take effect if the injunction is lifted or overturned on appeal. If ultimately implemented, the rule would represent one of the most significant changes to the administration of F, J, and I nonimmigrant status in decades. By replacing the longstanding Duration of Status (D/S) framework with fixed periods of admission, it would fundamentally alter how affected individuals maintain lawful status in the United States and would impose substantial new compliance, monitoring, and filing obligations on foreign nationals, educational institutions, exchange program sponsors, foreign media organizations, and employers.

Accordingly, organizations with affected populations should continue to assess the potential impact of the rule on workforce planning, employee mobility programs, and immigration compliance processes. In particular, employers may need to prepare for an increase in extension filings, additional administrative burdens, and enhanced tracking of immigration status expiration dates to ensure continued compliance.

We will continue to monitor developments in the litigation and provide updates as additional information becomes available. In the meantime, please contact your Seyfarth immigration team with any questions regarding the potential impact of these developments on your organization or workforce.

Federal immigration officials then began removal proceedings, arguing that the conviction made him inadmissible because he had committed a crime involving moral turpitude.
The statute applies when a permanent resident "has committed" a covered offense, Thomas wrote, rather than only after a conviction has been entered.
It did not say how much evidence border officers need when making the initial determination.
text:
The Supreme Court has given immigration officials more authority over some green card holders reentering the United States while facing criminal charges, ruling that border officers do not need clear and convincing evidence of a qualifying crime when the resident arrives.

The 6-3 decision in Blanche v. Lau allows the government to establish that evidence later during removal proceedings. The ruling overturns a federal appeals court decision that imposed the higher proof requirement at the border.

Justice Clarence Thomas wrote the majority opinion, joined by Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan dissented.

The ruling reverses a federal appeals court that found the government needed clear and convincing evidence at the border before it could treat a returning permanent resident as seeking admission under one of the exceptions in federal immigration law.

Lau, a Chinese citizen, became a lawful permanent resident in 2007. New Jersey charged him with trademark counterfeiting in May 2012. While the criminal case was pending, he traveled to China and returned to John F. Kennedy International Airport the following month.

Green card holders returning from temporary trips abroad are generally treated as already admitted to the United States. Federal law creates several exceptions, including when a lawful permanent resident has committed certain crimes involving moral turpitude.

When Lau returned, a border officer relied on the pending counterfeiting charge and treated him as an applicant seeking admission. Officials paroled him into the country while the criminal case continued.

Lau later pleaded guilty to trademark counterfeiting. Federal immigration officials then began removal proceedings, arguing that the conviction made him inadmissible because he had committed a crime involving moral turpitude.

An immigration judge ordered Lau removed, and the Board of Immigration Appeals upheld the decision. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit later sided with Lau, finding that immigration officials needed clear and convincing evidence when he returned that he had already committed a qualifying offense.

The Supreme Court rejected that requirement.

Thomas wrote that the Immigration and Nationality Act does not impose the clear and convincing evidence standard on border officers making the initial decision about how to treat a returning permanent resident.

The majority said the government may establish the necessary facts later in removal proceedings. Lau's guilty plea supplied that evidence, according to the Court.

The justices also rejected Lau's argument that officials had to wait for a criminal conviction before treating him as seeking admission. The statute applies when a permanent resident "has committed" a covered offense, Thomas wrote, rather than only after a conviction has been entered.

The Court left one issue unresolved. It did not say how much evidence border officers need when making the initial determination. The justices held only that the clear and convincing evidence standard imposed by the Second Circuit does not apply at that stage.

The ruling affects lawful permanent residents who travel abroad while facing criminal allegations, because being treated as an applicant for admission can change the rules governing detention, parole, and later removal proceedings.

Jackson focused on those consequences in dissent. Joined by Sotomayor and Kagan, she argued that officials should have to establish that a statutory exception applies before changing how a returning permanent resident is treated at the border.

She also pointed to Lau's experience after officials confiscated his physical green card and issued temporary documentation while his immigration case remained unresolved.

text:
Why It Matters

A new Congressional Research Service’s analysis places Temporary Protected Status at the center of a fast-moving policy shift under the Trump administration. Congress created TPS in 1990 to provide safe haven to noncitizens in the United States, regardless of immigration status, who are nationals of countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disaster, or other extraordinary circumstances that prevent their safe return.

When President Trump took office in January 2025, 17 countries had TPS designations, and by September 10, 2026, TPS had been terminated for 13 of them.

For Congress, the report frames a question about how much of the program’s future will be determined through executive designations, extensions, and terminations rather than through new legislation. For people covered by TPS, the timing of each announcement can determine how long protection and work authorization continue.

The Big Picture

The Secretary of DHS may designate a country for six, 12, or 18 months and may extend the designation if the country continues to meet the conditions for designation. The same framework requires termination when the Secretary determines that a country no longer meets those conditions.

The listed beneficiary counts included 353,160 people for Haiti, 70,070 for Honduras, and 627,750 across Venezuela’s concurrent 2021 and 2023 designations. Other country-specific counts in the report were 11,740 for Afghanistan, 12,160 for Nepal, 6,100 for Syria, 5,460 for Cameroon, and 5,010 for Ethiopia. The remaining counts were 3,970 for Burma, 3,850 for Nicaragua, 2,810 for Yemen, 1,080 for Somalia, and 230 for South Sudan.

The Bottom Line

As of September 10, TPS designations for El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine, and Lebanon remained in effect.

El Salvador’s designation was set to expire on September 9, but no Federal Register notice had announced a termination or extension as of the following day. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services alert posted September 9 said an announcement on El Salvador's TPS would come later. Until that announcement, Salvadoran individuals covered by TPS retained protection and work authorization.

Sudan and Ukraine were set to reach their expiration date on October 19, while Lebanon’s designation was set to expire on November 27.

text:
Fifteen sheriffs across New York say the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act limits their control. On Tuesday, they rallied to halt enforcement of the law while a federal judge considers their lawsuit against Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James.

The sheriffs are challenging restrictions related to 287(g) agreements and argue the law is an overreach of authority. They are asking the court to pause enforcement until the case is heard.

“I don't participate in the 287(g) agreement. I have my own reasons, but politics should not be playing any part in this,” Jefferson County Sheriff Peter Barnett said.

Although his county has never made formal partnerships with ICE, Barnett said limitations on who authorities can work with will make it harder to do the job.

"I should be able to, and will, governor, cooperate with any agency legally enforcing the law," said Barnett.

The Federation for American Immigration Reform represents Barnett and the 14 other sheriffs in the lawsuit against Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James. The group's director of investigations, Mateo Forero, said the state's argument that the law conserves local resources does not accurately describe the legislation.

“That is why we sued and why we have asked the court for an emergency order. We want to freeze the status quo. That means keeping the written 287(g) agreements that these sheriffs had as of the day the law became effective,” Forero said.

A preliminary injunction involving 287(g) agreements similar to the one being sought in this case was previously attempted by the U.S. Department of Justice. A federal court denied that motion.

When asked how this lawsuit differs from that effort, Forero said, “In our lawsuit, we have now brought a mountain of evidence, including six sworn declarations from several of our sheriffs.”

CBS6 reached out to the governor's office and the attorney general's office to ask whether enforcement of the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act would be paused while the case proceeds. The attorney general's office said enforcement will not be paused and noted that it is suing Rensselaer County and the county sheriff's office for alleged noncompliance with the law.

Forero said all documents from the plaintiffs' side had been filed as of Tuesday and that they are awaiting either a court decision or a hearing. He also said FAIR is handling the lawsuit against the governor and attorney general on a pro bono basis and is partially funding the lawsuit against Rensselaer County.

title: 'Alligator Alcatraz' detainees were held in cages the size of a phone booth - Florida Phoenix
authors: Kate Payne, The Florida Trib, Kate Payne, The Florida Trib, Jay Waagmeester, Mitch Perry, Liv Caputo
description:
The report gives a rare glimpse into the sprawling makeshift facility that was built in a matter of days by Gov.
Democratic state lawmakers and outside observers were barred from inspecting the compound, which, along with another state-run immigration detention center, carries an estimated $1 billion price tag.
Asked about the inspector general’s findings at a news conference Monday, DeSantis said he hadn’t read the report but defended Florida’s unprecedented work to carry out federal immigration enforcement.
At the time, federal officials said detainees were transferred out of “Alligator Alcatraz” because of hurricane-season safety concerns.
