title: Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' confined migrants in 'small metal enclosures': DHS internal watchdog
description:
The report describes alarming conditions, including unhygienic practices for food and water as well as limited opportunities for migrants to bathe themselves.
OIG found that in at least one documented case, a migrant was put in the small cages as a punishment.
The report generated swift blowback from immigration advocates who targeted ICE’s explanation for the small cages.
“Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG.
Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and well-being,” the watchdog wrote.
text:
A new report reviewing the conditions at the now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” center in Florida slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for failing to meet a variety of federal standards, describing “unprecedented” treatment of migrants, including containing them in cages about the size of a phone booth.

The Monday report from the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) is the first such federal review of the facility, which is referred to in the report as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF).

The report describes alarming conditions, including unhygienic practices for food and water as well as limited opportunities for migrants to bathe themselves.

OIG said Alligator Alcatraz provided half the living space for migrants required under federal law — just 28 square feet when the facility was at max capacity, far from the 75-square-foot mandate.

ICE officials also used cages that were roughly 4 feet by 4 feet as “‘calming areas’ for detainees to deescalate and have time alone.”

“FSSF confined 79 detainees in small metal enclosures — each offering about 18 square feet of floor space — for periods ranging from several minutes to nearly 2 hours, a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities. The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” OIG wrote.

OIG found that in at least one documented case, a migrant was put in the small cages as a punishment.

The report generated swift blowback from immigration advocates who targeted ICE’s explanation for the small cages.

“There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike,” Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of refugee settlement agency Global Refuge, said in a statement.

“The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food, and basic hygiene — and in at least one case locked in a cage as punishment. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty, carried out in our name and on our dime, to the tune of more than a million dollars a day.”

OIG said they were unable to “independently confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding their use of the enclosures” as well as other allegations, such as deprivation of food or water issues described in a prior Amnesty International report, as none of the detainees interviewed while OIG was there reported those conditions.

“Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG. Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and well-being,” the watchdog wrote.

Both ICE and DHS did not immediately respond to request for comment.

In the report, however, the agency and department placed much of the responsibility for the facility on Florida, despite it being constructed with federal funds and managed by ICE agents.

“While FEMA [Federal Emergency Management Agency] provided funding for the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF) under the Shelter and Services Program, DHS did not have a contract with Florida to manage the detention space within the facility. The State of Florida authorized the repurposing of the center from the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport into a state detention center,” DHS officials wrote in a letter in response to the report.

Other aspects also generated significant attention from inspectors.

Several detainees told OIG investigators they did not have access to clean water, saying that self-serve water stations were dirty. Migrants were also given a cup but said they had no way to wash it.

Some were also only scheduled to shower three days a week, and the report includes photos of the showers covered in bugs.

Updated at 3:17 p.m. EDT.

title: ICE deported a gay Brazilian man to Equatorial Guinea. Now he's gone silent.
authors: John Washington/LOOKOUT, John Washington, Jerod MacDonald-Evoy
description:
Hotel Bamy in Equatorial Guinea is not a prison, but Pietro Graza hasn’t been able to leave for weeks.
Graza was almost killed by police partly because he is a gay man, and immigrated to the states where he sought asylum.
He was then flown to Liberia, and finally moved to the Hotel Bamy in Equatorial Guinea.
While homosexuality is not illegal in Equatorial Guinea, repression and persecution of the queer community is common, and the state’s willingness to impose harsh or extralegal penalties makes the situation even more dangerous.
When the plane landed again, they were in Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea.
text:
Hotel Bamy in Equatorial Guinea is not a prison, but Pietro Graza hasn’t been able to leave for weeks. He has been held captive in the semi-abandoned luxury hotel in Malabo, the former capital city, after being deported from Arizona despite legally seeking protections in the United States for protection against torture in his home country of Brazil.

Graza was almost killed by police partly because he is a gay man, and immigrated to the states where he sought asylum. But in 2024, he was detained by federal agents and held in a Florida detention camp before a transfer to Eloy Detention Center. He was then flown to Liberia, and finally moved to the Hotel Bamy in Equatorial Guinea. He has no ties to the country or the continent.

Now he and about a dozen other men and women are trapped in legal limbo. He and the others were sent, in chains, to the small, oil-rich Central African petrostate, which has been run for more than four decades by one of the world’s most repressive governments.

While homosexuality is not illegal in Equatorial Guinea, repression and persecution of the queer community is common, and the state’s willingness to impose harsh or extralegal penalties makes the situation even more dangerous. According to a 2023 State Department Country Report on Equatorial Guinea, “Security forces reportedly subjected LGBTQI+ individuals to violence, including rape and other sexual violence, within the military and in jails and prisons.”

LOOKOUT spoke to Graza via WhatsApp audio messages in Spanish, as well as by video call with assistance from a Portuguese interpreter.

His story illustrates a growing trend in U.S. immigration enforcement in which, if the federal government can’t deport someone to their home country because they’ve been granted protection or because the government of the home country is unwilling to accept them, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been finding other places to deport them to: what’s referred to as “third-country deportations.” And for LGBTQ+ prisoners who legally can’t be sent back to their home countries because of the possibility of death, torture or imprisonment, many of them end up back there anyway.

‘Shoot him!’

According to Third Country Deportation Watch, the United States has agreements with at least 35 other countries and has deported more than 26,000 people to them since the start of the second Trump administration.

One common fear among those deported to third countries is that they could subsequently be deported back to their home country anyway — a process known as “chain refoulement” — where they could face persecution, imprisonment or death. Other serious concerns are language barriers, further criminalization, and a lack of connections or support people may find in these third countries.

Recent reporting from The Advocate raises concerns about specifically deporting LGBTQ+ people to countries where they could face criminalization, detention, torture or death. “Many of the countries on those [third country] lists have terrible track records when it comes to the rights of LGBTQ+ people,” said Kate O’Donnell, an attorney with the Tucson-based law firm Green Evans-Schroeder that represents both Graza and Ahmed Soliman — a gay man from Egypt who lived in Tucson, was captured by ICE and then deported to the hotel in Equatorial Guinea.

She said that Graza and Soliman face “de facto criminalization” and the potential for “terrible violence” because of their sexual identity.

Shortly after Graza arrived, Guinean officials told him they would facilitate his departure to Brazil. “That’s where my life is at risk,” Graza said.

On Sept. 8, armed police officers came to his room. They forced him to hand over his phone — his only lifeline to his lawyer — as well as the outside world. It was the second time in a few days that guards had moved against the detainees held at the hotel. Two nights earlier, police pointed assault rifles at two of the men during a dispute over an earlier round of confiscated phones, an incident first reported by Reuters.

One guard, pointing his rifle at one of the men, yelled, “Shoot him!”

“Several armed police officers came to my room this morning, around 8 o’clock, to take my phone because of that interview I gave on Sunday. The worst part is that my life is at risk, because my phone contains the contact details of various journalists who have interviewed me,” Graza said in the last voice message he was able to deliver to an attorney helping him on his case, using a borrowed phone.

Graza has been unreachable since.

The day after Graza and the others had their phones confiscated, Soliman was arrested. His attorney doesn’t know what the charges against Soliman are or where he is now being held, and doesn’t know if Graza, Soliman or others were beaten. But reportedly, some of the people held in the hotel have “cuts and bruises,” a person on the ground relayed to Soliman’s attorney.

From a supplement store in Brazil to a coma

Graza’s account of what drove him from Brazil began, he said, with a small nutritional supplement store he opened around 2014. He also has a degree in teaching and specializes in literature. Running the store was, in his telling, meant to be a modest side hustle connected to his gym life.

Local police officers who controlled protection rackets in the area, he said, wanted him to pay into what shopkeepers referred to as a security fund — a collection extorted from business owners in exchange for “protection.” Graza refused, even though police told him he needed extra protection because he was gay.

Combined with what he described as their contempt for his sexual orientation, he said the officers began threatening him.

Graza said a cousin who was a police officer intervened and warned him that officers were fabricating a case to have him arrested for selling steroids. He hired a lawyer and was able to avoid arrest.

Weeks later, he said, two men on a motorcycle opened fire on him outside his home. He survived but lost a kidney, lost the use of much of his right arm and spent time in a coma. He underwent multiple surgeries and said he eventually recovered about 90% of his mobility. He said the shooting was never meaningfully investigated and claimed police erased the evidence in his case. A deputy separately demanded the equivalent of $4,000 in local currency to make the steroid case disappear. He refused to pay the bribe.

If he is sent back to Brazil, he said, the same officers he accused will know immediately.

“Because when I return to Brazil, the police will identify me,” he said. “They will know that I returned. They will know that I’m alive.”

‘This goes against all human rights.’

Graza said he and his then-partner had traveled to the U.S. periodically for years before the shooting, including trips to Florida. After his recovery, still dealing with depression and panic attacks stemming from the attack, he applied for a student visa to study in the United States.

Soon after arriving, he said, he discovered his partner had been unfaithful. He decided to stay in the U.S. under his partner’s household for the first year but eventually sought independence. But that was difficult, he said, because of the cost of the medications he needed for both his kidney condition and his deteriorating mental health. He said he hit a depressive low, had panic attacks and began using drugs. He was caught by police with methamphetamines. His visa had expired at that point, and after serving a short sentence, when he was due to be released, ICE was waiting for him.

Graza’s asylum fight ran through two detention centers over nearly two years. ICE transferred him from Baker County Jail near Jacksonville, Florida, to Eloy Detention Center in Arizona in the summer of 2025.

He would spend roughly the next year at the Eloy Detention Center, while lawyers with the University of Miami’s asylum clinic built a case using Brazilian court and police records — including documentation, he said, that the officers who had tried to kill him were later arrested on unrelated corruption charges.

On April 16, 2026, an immigration judge ruled in his favor and gave him protected status under the Convention Against Torture, or CAT, agreement. But that didn’t mean he was being released.

“ICE asked for three months to continue keeping me detained because they wanted to find a country to send me to,” he said. He said a government representative later asked him to sign a document agreeing to be sent to Liberia. On his lawyers’ instructions, he refused to sign it.

Within days, he said, he was moved anyway.

Of the few dozen people forced onto the flight to Liberia, he said, three refused to comply — a Mexican man, a Cuban man and an Ethiopian man. Officers responded, he said, with a restraint he described as similar to a device called the WRAP, which has been criticized for inflicting torturous pain and causing asphyxiation. He called the restraint “brutal.”

“When we saw what they did to those three people, nobody else wanted to resist anymore, because it was so horrible, so violent,” he said. “How can someone do that? This goes against all human rights.”

What followed, he said, was a 36-hour flight, shackled the whole time.

ICE did not immediately respond to a detailed list of questions about Graza’s treatment during his deportation.

“It was a situation of terror, because inside the plane we remained handcuffed,” he said. “It lasted 36 hours, and it was extremely uncomfortable. You really felt like human garbage.”

Messages gone quiet

When the deportation plane landed in Liberia, Graza and a small group refused to get off the plane, resisting the agents trying to force them out. That scuffle was documented by a bystander and reported on by The New York Times.

Ground crew and officials moved the group onto the tarmac to negotiate and described being pressured to accept resettlement in a third country.

“We were terrified,” he said.

Graza said he and the others who resisted were loaded back onto the same plane, with ICE agents saying they were being sent back to the United States.

When the plane landed again, they were in Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea.

Still restrained, he said, hooded officers pulled the group from the plane and forced them into cars.

“We were handcuffed by our feet and hands,” Graza said. “Even so, the police with machine guns grabbed us and threw us into the cars, one person holding each of us. We were completely helpless. This was around midnight, behind the airport, everything dark. Don’t you understand how terrifying that is? You just wanted to cry because of the desperation. The women were screaming. It was the worst scene I have ever witnessed in my life.”

The convoy delivered Graza and the rest of the group to the decommissioned hotel in Malabo, where he remained until at least Sept. 9 — a building he insists, despite officials’ repeated denials, functions as a detention center.

That is where Graza and others remain, now without any means to communicate and thousands of miles from anything — or anybody — they know.

WhatsApp messages sent to Graza since Sept. 9 have gone unread.

text:
The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court also issued the judge a formal reprimand

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement condemning a Massachusetts judge who had allowed an illegal alien to use a back exit in her courtroom to escape U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

On April 2, 2018, illegal alien Oscar Manuel Peguero, alias Jose Medina-Perez, went to court after being arrested for possession of a Class B controlled substance and possession of a Class E controlled substance in Newton, Massachusetts. He also had an outstanding warrant at the time in Pennsylvania for being a fugitive from justice. The presiding judge was Massachusetts State District Court Judge Shelley Joseph. ICE lodged a detainer for Peguero on March 30, the same day he was arrested, but the detainer was not honored.

While an ICE officer was waiting outside the courtroom to arrest Peguero, Judge Joseph let Peguero leave the courtroom through a back exit that allowed him to evade ICE custody.

Image

Oscar Manuel Peguero, AKA Jose Medina-Perez

In 2019, Joseph was charged with conspiracy to obstruct justice, aiding and abetting obstruction of justice, and aiding and abetting obstruction of a federal proceeding. In 2022, the Biden Administration dropped the charges against Joseph.

On September 10, 2026, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court (SJC) issued Joseph a formal reprimand. The SJC found that she “created an appearance of impropriety in violation of her duties” when she ordered the court clerk to shut off the court’s audio recording systems during the proceedings.

“This judicial misconduct reflects what DHS is facing across the country,” said DHS General Counsel James Percival. “Certain judges think it is their duty to undermine, rather than enforce, federal immigration law. Helping illegal aliens escape from immigration officers is a felony. Sanctuary politicians and sanctuary judges alike are on notice.”

Peguero first illegally entered the United States through Boston Logan International Airport in January 2003, falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen. He was arrested and deported on January 31, 2003. He then illegally re-entered the United States – a felony – through New Mexico in April 2007. He was arrested by the U.S. Border Patrol and deported a second time on June 22, 2007. He then illegally entered the United States for a THIRD time at an unknown date and location.

title: AG Brown sues to block new public charge rule from U.S. Department of Homeland Security
description:
Attorney General Nick Brown today joined 21 other states and the District of Columbia in suing to halt the new public charge rule from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which would allow immigration officials to punish immigrants for lawful use of public benefits.
The new policy would give immigration officers broad discretion to deny green cards based on use of public benefits.
The lawsuit argues that the disruption will not stop with the families who disenroll from public benefits.
The attorneys general are asking a federal judge to declare the 2026 public charge rule unlawful and vacate it, protecting states and their residents from its unlawful harms.
Joining Brown in filing this lawsuit, which was led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, and Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, are the attorneys general of Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, and the governor of Pennsylvania.
text:
Attorney General Nick Brown today joined 21 other states and the District of Columbia in suing to halt the new public charge rule from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which would allow immigration officials to punish immigrants for lawful use of public benefits.

The new policy would give immigration officers broad discretion to deny green cards based on use of public benefits. The coalition is asking the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York to declare this rule unlawful.

“This new rule is designed to intimidate and harm immigrant families,” Brown said. “But DHS cannot legally withhold permanent residency from people who receive benefits to which they’re lawfully entitled, like food assistance, even for a short period of time.”

A "public charge" means a person who is likely to become primarily dependent on the government for long-term subsistence. In 2022, the federal government issued a rule limiting the focus of public charge determinations to whether applicants for admission were likely to depend on publicly funded cash assistance or need long-term institutionalization at government expense. The new DHS rule taking effect Sept. 18 would let immigration officers count nearly any means-tested public benefit, used for any length of time, against an applicant. The rule also allows immigration officers to consider some benefits legally used by family members whom the applicant is legally obligated to support, even if the family member is a U.S. citizen. There is no clear limit on which benefits or how much use count against an applicant, leaving families to guess which forms of assistance might put their immigration status at risk.

The administration has acknowledged the new rule will likely cause fear and confusion among immigrant families and lead them to disenroll from benefits to which they are legally entitled, the coalition argues in its complaint. DHS estimates that disenrollment or forgone enrollment resulting from the new rule could reduce federal Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program transfer payments to the states by more than $4 billion annually and federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) transfer payments by more than $1 billion annually.

The lawsuit argues that the disruption will not stop with the families who disenroll from public benefits. When people lose access to health coverage, they delay care and turn to emergency rooms instead, straining safety-net hospitals and community health centers and raising costs for everyone. Schools risk losing automatic certification for free and reduced-price meal programs when SNAP and Medicaid enrollment drops below required thresholds, cutting off meals for eligible students regardless of income or immigration status. Federal Title I education funding is also likely to fall if student enrollment in benefits decreases and would be a devastating loss for schools. Reduced participation in SNAP can also harm local economies, draining money from the grocery stores and local businesses that depend on SNAP recipients’ business.

The coalition notes that the states and local governments that administer these programs will bear direct costs, from new communications to staff training to information technology changes needed to manage the disruption. This is on top of the added strain of residents cycling on and off programs out of fear.

The coalition argues that the new rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it is arbitrary and capricious, exceeds DHS’s statutory authority, and departs from the longstanding meaning of the public charge provision established by Congress.

The attorneys general are asking a federal judge to declare the 2026 public charge rule unlawful and vacate it, protecting states and their residents from its unlawful harms.

Joining Brown in filing this lawsuit, which was led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, and Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, are the attorneys general of Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, and the governor of Pennsylvania. The lawsuit was filed alongside a coalition of cities and counties led by the City of New York.

text:
Small metal enclosures measuring just 18 square feet, severe overcrowding, dirty drinking water, and bug-infested showers are detailed in a scathing watchdog report released by the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General.

The unannounced inspection of the Florida Soft-Sided Facility—informally known as "Alligator Alcatraz"—in Ochopee revealed severe violations of basic human safety and hygiene standards while the facility was operational.

'Unprecedented' Metal Enclosures

Inspectors found that between July 2025 and January 2026, 79 immigration detainees were locked in tiny, 4-foot-3-inch by 4-foot-3-inch metal structures—offering roughly 18 square feet of floor space—for up to nearly two hours at a time.

Facility staff claimed the small metal structures were voluntary "calming areas" for detainees to "reflect on their behavior choices," but federal oversight officials paint a far different picture:

Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among detention facilities OIG has inspected and presents significant risks to detainee health and safety."

Documentation obtained by inspectors revealed at least one instance where a detainee was locked inside an enclosure for 26 minutes for failing "to comply with a lawful command," contradicting staff claims that the cages were non-punitive.

Severe Overcrowding & Lack of Basic Hygiene

The watchdog report outlined cramped, windowless living conditions where they were trapped inside fenced units for most of their day. The facility provided just 28 sq. ft. of floor space per person -- less than half of the 75 sq. ft. minimum required under Florida standards.

Other findings from the report outlining inhumane conditions:

Bug Infestations: Inspection photos showed shower facility ceilings infested with small insects. Detainees were restricted to showering only three days a week.

Contaminated Water Concerns: Six out of eight interviewed detainees reported they lacked access to clean drinking water, describing it as "dirty" and noting they had no way to wash their plastic drinking cups.

Rationed Hygiene Supplies: Detainees were only allowed to keep a toothbrush in their housing units; to use toothpaste on non-shower days, staff had to apply it to their brushes directly.

Spoiled Food Risks: Walk-in freezers holding perishable meals were recorded operating at 14F, well above the required 0F safety limit, creating significant risks of foodborne illness.

Confusion Over Authority

Inspectors noted a chaotic regulatory environment, citing a facility official who admitted it was "so gray as to whose place this is... and which standards to follow."

While the Department of Homeland Security argued that the State of Florida maintained authority over day-to-day operations under 287(g) agreements, federal auditors noted that the site was funded with over $608 million in federal FEMA grant money and exclusively housed ICE immigration detainees.

Although all 10 corrective recommendations were administratively closed after FSSF permanently shut down in June 2026, the Inspector General warned that similar unchecked conditions remain a concern at other state-run facilities currently operating in Florida.

There is no clear limit on which benefits, or how much use, count against an applicant, leaving families to guess which forms of assistance might put their immigration status at risk.

Attorney General Clark and the coalition assert that the Administration has acknowledged that fear and confusion about the new rule would cause immigrant families to disenroll from benefits to which they are legally entitled. DHS estimates that disenrollment or forgone enrollment resulting from the new rule could reduce federal Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) transfer payments to the states by approximately $4 billion annually and federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, known in Vermont as 3SquaresVT) transfer payments by approximately $1 billion annually.

The lawsuit argues that the disruption will not stop with the families who disenroll from public benefits. When people lose access to health coverage, they delay care and turn to emergency rooms instead, straining hospitals and community health centers, and raising costs for everyone. Schools risk losing automatic certification for free and reduced-price meal programs when SNAP and Medicaid enrollment drops below required thresholds, cutting off meals for eligible students regardless of income or immigration status.

Federal Title I education funding is also likely to fall if student enrollment in benefits decreases and would be a devastating loss for schools. Reduced participation in SNAP can also harm local economies, draining money from the grocery stores and local businesses that depend on SNAP recipients’ business.

The coalition notes that the states and local governments that administer these programs will bear direct costs, from new communications to staff training to information technology changes needed to manage the disruption. This is on top of the added strain of residents cycling on and off programs out of fear.

Attorney General Clark and the coalition argue that the new rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it is arbitrary and capricious, exceeds DHS’s statutory authority, and departs from the longstanding meaning of the public charge provision established by Congress. The attorneys general are asking a federal judge to declare the 2026 public charge rule unlawful and vacate it, protecting states and their residents from its unlawful harms.

A copy of the complaint is HERE(link is external).

Joining Attorney General Clark in filing this lawsuit are the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, the District of Columbia, and the governor of Pennsylvania.

Today’s lawsuit is the 70th case Attorney General Clark has brought against the Trump Administration since President Trump took office in January 2025. For more information on actions taken by the Attorney General on behalf of Vermonters, see website(link is external).

text:
A coalition of Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration to block a rule that makes it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards or even enter the country if they rely on public benefits.

The 22 states and D.C. are challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) “public charge” rule, set to take effect Friday.

The states, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), argue the rule will penalize immigrants and their families for using public benefits like food stamps, Medicaid or housing vouchers to which they are legally entitled.

“Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” James said in a statement. “This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled.”

The lawsuit argues that under the rule, immigrants would need to stop using public assistance programs to meet their basic needs or risk being denied green cards in the future.

Noncitizens and family members would disenroll from programs, even though they are eligible, and the states argued they will lose billions of dollars in federal funding.

They said the rule is “arbitrary and capricious” and that the DHS both ignored the harmful consequences of the change and failed to adequately justify it.

“As households forgo their legal access to benefits—such as preventative healthcare, nutritional assistance, and school lunch—public health, local economies, public education, and public safety will suffer. The Final Rule will increase the prevalence of disease, drive up the costs of medical care, and increase poverty,” the lawsuit argued.

A separate lawsuit challenging the rule was filed by a group of local governments, led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D).

The Trump administration argues the rule is necessary to protect American taxpayers from subsidizing immigrants who may become dependent on public benefits.

The law focuses only on immigrants who are lawfully present and eligible to apply for permanent residency. Immigrants who are in the country illegally are not eligible for public benefits.

The final rule is a revival of a similar policy that the administration tried to impose during President Trump’s first term before it was met with legal challenges and later reversed by the Biden administration.

So-called “public charge” restrictions that bar immigrants from obtaining green cards if they are likely to rely on government assistance have been part of federal immigration policy for more than 140 years, but they have long focused only on cash benefit programs.

The Trump administration’s first attempt to change the rule broadened the types of benefits to include the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, most Medicaid benefits and certain housing programs.

The new rule has no limits of what can be considered, saying only the DHS “will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits.”

For example, if a U.S. citizen child uses state-provided health insurance, that can be used against a noncitizen parent to deny them a green card. Officers could also count a child’s participation in a school’s free lunch program against their noncitizen parent’s application for citizenship.

“The final rule puts families in the untenable position of choosing between a U.S. citizen child’s access to healthcare, and their noncitizen parent’s ability to remain in the country,” the lawsuit argued.

The states’ suit was brought by the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Nevada, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, along with the governor of Pennsylvania.

Alongside New York City, the local lawsuit was brought by Chicago; the City and County of San Francisco; Santa Clara County, Calif.; Seattle; and King County, Wash.

title: DHS report: Alligator Alcatraz detainees were kept in phone booth-sized outdoor cages
description:

The report also found that the facility did not comply with food safety standards, with perishable food kept above the recommended temperature.
“Before showering, facility staff give detainees a personal hygiene kit with soap, shampoo, deodorant, a toothbrush, and toothpaste,” the report said.
The OIG made 10 recommendations to the facility to ensure compliance with standards, but Alligator Alcatraz closed in June, so all have been administratively closed.

text:
TAMPA, Fla. (WFLA) — A new report from the Department of Homeland Security’s Inspector General found that some immigration detainees at the now-shuttered Alligator Alcatraz facility were confined to outdoor cages just slightly larger than phone booths for more than an hour at a time.

The office stopped by the Everglades detention center unannounced for an inspection on Jan. 21, 2026, and noted an “absence of well-defined standards” for holding detainees on immigration-related charges. The report quotes an unnamed facility official, who said it was “so gray as to whose place this is…and which standards to follow.”

On the day of the inspection, each unit contained between 22 and 31 detainees. Investigators found that detainees in the most packed units were provided about 28 square feet of living space per person, which was less than half of what was required, “creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units.”

To satisfy the minimum square footage requirement, each unit would need to house no more than 11 detainees, which was approximately one-third of the current capacity.

Concerns over lack of space were identified throughout the facility. The report said that between July 17, 2025, and January 18, 2026, 79 people were kept in small metal enclosures, with about 18 square feet of floor space, for an average duration of about an hour. Some were held for up to two hours, which was the maximum time allowed under posted standards, in a space that measured approximately 4 feet 3 inches, by 4 feet 3 inches, and 7 feet 9 inches tall.

Investigators described the use of these cages as “a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities.”

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report said.

Facility staff described the cages, which were placed in the outdoor recreation area, as “calming areas,” and said detainees were closely monitored and were not locked inside. OIG inspectors reported that the cages had locking mechanisms on them.

The lack of clarity regarding standards meant detainees did not have access to services like a commissary, in-person family visits, or typical recreation resources, like televisions or playing cards in their housing units. Detainees in the Special Management Units, who were housed separately from others, did not have access to legal services and reported not being allowed to contact attorneys. One detainee reported being held for eight days in the SMU without recreation.

The report also found that the facility did not comply with food safety standards, with perishable food kept above the recommended temperature. Detainees told investigators that they did not have access to clean drinking water and were not allowed to clean the plastic cups they drank out of.

People housed at the facility were only permitted to shower on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, which violates standards requiring daily access to showers. An insect infestation was observed in the ceiling of the showers.

“Before showering, facility staff give detainees a personal hygiene kit with soap, shampoo, deodorant, a toothbrush, and toothpaste,” the report said. “However, after showering, detainees may only bring the toothbrush back to their housing units. If detainees need more hygiene items on days when they do not shower, they must request them, and staff supervise their use.”

The report said that if a detainee requested toothpaste, a staff member would apply it to their toothbrush.

The OIG made 10 recommendations to the facility to ensure compliance with standards, but Alligator Alcatraz closed in June, so all have been administratively closed.

In a Monday news conference, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who brushed off reports of inhumane conditions while the facility was still operating, said he has not yet read the OIG report.

“They’re going to accuse you of mistreatment no matter what you do,” DeSantis said.

title: Truth #1: Truth-Telling About ICE-Related Human Rights Violations - Minnesota Women's Press

They followed me for about eight miles before pulling me over and arresting me,” said Orozco Verdusco.

She gave testimony about the day ICE swarmed upon Roosevelt High School in South Minneapolis on January 7, which was also the day ICE shot and killed Renée Good.
text:
“I’m taking this risk because I know we have to fight hard to make changes that we need, to make changes that we deserve,” said Eustaquio Orozco Verdusco, a Minnesota labor organizer who was abducted by ICE on January 9 during Operation Metro Surge. He was giving testimony at the Minnesota Truth Council on August 21, one of numerous people speaking about the ordeals they went through as a result of the federal crackdown.

On March 25, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz issued an executive order creating the “Governor’s Council to Record the Truth of Operation Metro Surge and Operation PARRIS,” also known as the Minnesota Truth Council. The goal of the Truth Council is to produce a historical record of experiences of Operation Metro Surge that will include a report with findings and recommendations for policymakers. Orozco Verdusco gave his testimony to the Truth Council at an event hosted by the Advocates for Human Rights, a nonprofit organization located in Minnesota that has been collecting stories since mid-May.

Orozco Verdusco said that when he first learned about Operation Metro Surge, he didn’t leave his house for more than 20 days. “I left because I had a work meeting. I was followed just a few blocks from our home. They followed me for about eight miles before pulling me over and arresting me,” said Orozco Verdusco.

He says the next day they were flown to Texas. “After 72 hours we were told we could talk to our families which didn’t happen. Three or four days later we had the opportunity to talk to them for three minutes. Only three minutes,” he said. Three weeks later, they were moved to New Mexico. “During that move, we were given no food, no drinks, all day and night,” he continued. “They stopped at a gas station. They got food, they got drinks, they ate and drank in front of us. They said when we arrived we would be given food and drinks. Well it was not that way. It wasn’t until the next morning that we could have breakfast. Finally we could call our families and talk for a little bit longer. When I talked to my family they told me my lawyer had presented a habeas corpus which had been denied. Every time I had an opportunity to talk to my family, they were telling me stories about people, organizations, communities, supporting me.”

Orozco Verdusco was released in June after being in detention for almost six months. In May, a federal judge ordered that anyone who was in the process of obtaining a T or U visa should be taken out of detention. A T or U visa enables immigrants who are victims of trafficking to remain in the U.S. for a period of time and grants them protections. Because Orozco Verdusco and his wife are in the process of getting a T visa, he was released.

“This is a bad moment we are living in, but it’s going to be better because of the people that live here,” he said. “I’m thankful to all those who prayed for me to come back, to join my family again.”

The event where Orozco Verdusco spoke took place at the first ever Convergence for Democracy at the Minneapolis Convention Center in downtown Minneapolis, Minn. The Convergence, hosted by Tending the Soil and co-sponsored by May Day Strong and Freedom Trainers, served as a national gathering for labor, community, faith, and legal advocates devoted to defending democracy in a moment of increasing authoritarianism and fascism. Speakers iterated that defending democracy means defending each other. The gathering was full of learning and trading resistance stories, and the opposition and resistance to Operation Metro Surge was highlighted in many of those stories.

Testimony About Public Schools

Six more people testified to the Truth Council at the Convergence, including Christin Crabtree, a grassroots community organizer and Minneapolis resident and parent who cofounded Minneapolis Families for Public Schools. She gave testimony about the day ICE swarmed upon Roosevelt High School in South Minneapolis on January 7, which was also the day ICE shot and killed Renée Good.

Crabtree says that she was at work the day that Renée Good was killed, and she had not planned to be at school dismissal, but showed up anyway. As students were exiting, a convoy of SUVs stopped in front of the main entrance of the school. “I ran faster than I ever had in my life,” said Crabtree. “I saw masked men with giant guns and in my mind visualized what had happened to Renée Good just hours before. Agents tackled our educators, aimed guns at our kids, and used chemical agents on our community, on our kids who were just trying to go home. I was mere inches from Greg Bovino. I remember the sound of a gun being cocked.”

Crabtree referenced the detention of Quentin Williams, an assistant teacher at Roosevelt who is now pursuing a lawsuit against the federal government after being tackled by agents. “He was a Black man being attacked by militarized police as high school students bore witness,” said Crabtree. “I felt echoes of 2020.”

Gabby Benavente Hobart is an educator at a high school in North Minneapolis working with Spanish-speaking students who are learning English and math. After the 2024 election, educators organized meetings to develop safety protocols for what to do if ICE showed up at school. “Still this preparation would not prepare us for the scale of the horror that was about to unfold,” said Benavente Hobart in her testimony to the Truth Council. “I am deeply grateful to my fellow educators at my side and in my union as well as community members in all walks of life.”

She recalled how one student apologized for having to log out of Zoom because ICE was in the street nearby. She shared how she consoled a mother whose son and husband were detained and separated by ICE. “To this day I think of him, how he was denied the joy of walking alongside classmates during graduation.”

ICE Detentions

Matt Allen is a local hip hop artist who goes by Nur-D. He gave testimony about his ICE detention after attending a protest after Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti.

“I watched on my phone as Alex Pretti was murdered in cold blood,” Allen said. “When I went out to have my voice be heard, I was attacked violently from behind by more than half a dozen men with guns who threw me to the street. They beat my body, they sprayed acid in my face, they told me I was being arrested for assaulting an officer, a charge I have yet to see.”

Allen said agents put him in a vehicle and he was released later. “We are living the worst case scenario,” he said. “What are you willing to do to stop it? They are killing people. And they will continue to capture and kill people not because a law says they can, but because they want to.”

Garrison Gibson Brown gave testimony about his arrest and time in ICE detention.

Gibson Brown said he was born in Liberia, that he has resided in the U.S. since he was four years old, and that he has been checking in with ICE regularly since 2009. He said on January 11, his family was woken up by ICE agents who had entered his house without a warrant and broke down the front door. The agents cuffed him in front of his family.

“After being at Whipple for a couple hours, the next morning they put some of us on a plane and sent us to Texas,” said Gibson Brown. “It was no better in Texas than it was at Whipple. The cells were dirty, the [correctional officers] they talk to you like you’re not human.”

Shot By an ICE Agent

On the day ICE agents shot and killed Renée Good, civil rights attorney Nicole Salonek Schladt was at Powderhorn Park bringing her child to therapy when she saw three large SUVs in the parking lot surrounded by masked agents. She approached the vehicles and noticed three teens huddled in the back seats. “They were all my children at that moment,” she said.

After an ICE agent told her to get out of the way, she began walking alongside the vehicle from a distance when another agent approached her from behind. “A gun appeared less than 12 inches from my face. I had no time to react, no time to panic,” she said. “The agent shot me in the face at point blank rage with what I learned were two projectile pepper balls. Everything went black. When I came to, lying in the snow, I could hardly breathe, I could hardly think.”

She vomited, removed all of her clothes, and was frothing at the mouth. “A park employee ushered me out of the cold into the rec center, a street medic emerged from literally nowhere and began flushing my eyes, a neighbor brought me a sheet and held it around my naked body,” she said. Her child’s therapist did breathing exercises and several people offered to share video recordings of the incident. It was then that they received news about Good’s killing.

“Another queer white woman, a mother like me, was dead, and I by the grace of God or something was not,” she said. Although she was alive, she experienced the impact of being shot by pepper balls, and was later diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury and cervical radiculopath that gave her nerve pain throughout her arms and hands. “My nail beds and scalp blistered,” she said. “I learned intimately why pepper ball projectiles are prohibited as chemical weapons in international armed conflict.”

In Central Minnesota

Benjamin gave testimony about his father who was detained and deported during Operation Metro Surge. He says he grew up in Honduras learning about movements for equality in the U.S. He says his father was often working with Fe y Justicia, a nonprofit in central Minnesota that provides training and clinics for community members.

On January 10, Benjamin says his father was driving when he was pulled over and his seatbelt was cut and he was abducted by masked men. After being detained, he was moved to Texas where his attorney had no jurisdiction, and then they moved him to New Mexico. “During the 43 days my dad spent in detention he tried to stay sane, he held back his tears because he did not want us to worry,” he says.

Eventually, his father was deported to Honduras. “When someone comes from a country where access to healthcare, freedom of speech is limited, I cannot blame my dad for wanting something different,” he said. “I’m not here to pretend my dad did not overstay his visa. I’m here to tell you that breaking an immigration rule should not take someone’s humanity away. Behind every case number, there is a person and behind them is a family loving them and waiting for them to be treated as a human being.”

Tending the Soil

Formed in 2018, Tending the Soil is an alignment of nonprofits and labor organizations in the Twin Cities that includes CTUL, Inquilinxs Unidxs por Justicia/Renters United for Justice, New Justice Project, SEIU Local 26, and Unidos MN. Cat Salonek Schladt, executive director of Tending the Soil, said that the goal of the conference was to build the national movement to resist authoritarianism. “We sit in the reality that the government is fueled by corporate greed that is killing everything in this young country,” she said in the opening plenary.

Ricardo Levins Morales, visual artist, organizer, and author based in Minneapolis, whose work inspired the name Tending the Soil, spoke during the closing plenary at the Convergence. “What we live under is a system for whom the basic hardline non-negotiable is the permanence of a permanent underclass. It cannot survive without that,” said Levins Morales. “Waves of movement ebb and flow, but they can still be part of a rising tide. People can often get really scared when a movement ebbs away and think, ‘oh it’s over now,’ when it could sometimes only be the first wave of a rising tide that will continue to climb. That’s what we’ve been experiencing.”

Amie Stager is the Associate Editor for Workday Magazine.

title: ICE arrests keep soaring. Here's why they are not leading to more deportations - KFGO
description:
About the same number of people were deported per day in May, for example, when there were around 19,000 fewer arrests, according to arrests data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a public records request and analyzed by Reuters.
The arrests include a growing number of people with no criminal conviction or charge and without deportation orders, according to the Deportation Data Project figures.
A lack of available flights and limits set by receiving countries have also capped Trump’s deportation ‌ambitions, former ​officials said.
Current and former officials said immigration officers are under growing pressure from the White House to hit a goal of 3,000 arrests per day.
Throughout the summer, ICE agents partnered with ​local police to conduct traffic stops and picked up people at homes and job sites.
text:
By Kristina Cooke and Ben Kellerman

Sept 14 (Reuters) – Immigration arrests in the U.S. have soared in recent months, aided by more local law enforcement cooperation with ICE, increased use of technology to track and process people, as well as enhanced data sharing between federal agencies.

But the mass arrest campaign this summer did not lead to a commensurate increase in deportations — according to preliminary U.S. government data reviewed by Reuters — a reflection of the legal and logistical limits faced by President Donald Trump as he attempts to hit his mass deportation ​goals.

Even as arrests jumped to nearly 51,000 in August, setting a record for a third straight month, deportation numbers held mostly steady, averaging around 1,200 per day, the preliminary government data ‌showed.

About the same number of people were deported per day in May, for example, when there were around 19,000 fewer arrests, according to arrests data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a public records request and analyzed by Reuters.

The disconnect is partly due to who is being targeted, five current and former officials said. The arrests include a growing number of people with no criminal conviction or charge and without deportation orders, according to the Deportation Data Project figures.

Many of those picked up had pending asylum or other legal claims – meaning they could not be immediately removed from the country unless they agreed to waive their rights and voluntarily depart.

A lack of available flights and limits set by receiving countries have also capped Trump’s deportation ‌ambitions, former ​officials said.

“This is a false narrative,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in response to questions from Reuters. “Thanks to President Trump’s strong immigration enforcement ⁠policies, three million illegals have left the United States.”

A WIDENING ⁠DRAGNET

The nationwide crackdown in recent months was not as high profile as past operations in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis, but it was more widespread.

“ICE Officers are herewith ordered … to do all in their power to achieve the very important goal of delivering the single largest Mass Deportation Program in History,” Trump declared on Truth Social in June.

Current and former officials said immigration officers are under growing pressure from the White House to hit a goal of 3,000 arrests per day.

“There are no quotas for arrests,” DHS said in a statement to Reuters.

Throughout the summer, ICE agents partnered with ​local police to conduct traffic stops and picked up people at homes and job sites. Others were detained at immigration courts or routine immigration appointments.

The administration continues to assert it is focused on the “worst of the worst,” but people with criminal convictions accounted for less than a quarter of arrests in July, the Deportation Data Project figures show. That figure was nearly 60% in December 2024, the month before Trump took ⁠office for a second time.

Among the easiest people to find are those who have shared their personal information with the ⁠U.S. government, hoping to achieve legal status. These include immigrants being sponsored for green cards by U.S. citizen family members, those with asylum claims – and the more ​than a million people who have had their temporary legal status revoked during Trump’s second term.

But those people often have active cases to stay in the United States, which can make it more difficult to quickly ​deport them.

Many also “have long roots in the United States and may be more likely to be able to quickly find a lawyer through their U.S. family members ‌and may be more aware of their rights,” said Julia Gelatt, an associate director at the Migration Policy Institute think tank.

At airports, following tips shared by the Transportation Security Administration, ICE has targeted people who had previously overstayed visas, even if they subsequently applied for asylum or married a U.S. citizen and had a path to legal status. More than 1,200 people were arrested by ICE following tips from TSA through early June, according to internal government data shared with Reuters.

Dolores Mendoza, 62, and Roberto Avalos, 64, were detained last week at an airport in Birmingham, Alabama, after returning from a trip to California to visit family. The couple entered the country ⁠on tourist visas in 2015, and stayed and adopted their three U.S. citizen grandchildren after their daughter died of breast cancer.

Neither has a criminal record. Both obtained work authorization and have pending petitions for permanent U.S. residence through their eldest grandchild, Marvin, who is now 22 and able to sponsor them.

Marvin said his younger brothers, ages 15 and 16, are struggling with their grandparents gone.

The youngest “hasn’t come out of his ⁠room often,” Marvin said. His other brother is “more angry than anything.”The couple’s lawyer has ‌filed a case in federal court contesting the detention as unlawful.

NOT ENOUGH PLANES

Some who can’t afford a lawyer have languished in detention.

Yajaira Moran, 50, has ⁠been held for the past five months despite having a pending claim for a crime victim visa as a survivor of domestic violence.

In early ​September, she gave up ‌and asked to go back to her home country of Nicaragua. She remains in detention as she waits to be deported.

Even when people are ​eligible for deportation, the ⁠logistics are complex, requiring coordination with receiving countries and transfers around a vast network of detention centers.

“Getting people on planes is really hard, and the actual number of available planes has historically been a choke point,” said Blas Nuñez-Neto, a former Biden administration official.

While the Trump administration signed a deal last year to purchase six Boeing 737 planes for deportations, those planes are still undergoing FAA checks and are not yet in use, according to a person briefed on the matter.

Planes in the existing fleet often depart without being at capacity, due to logistical, legal and diplomatic issues, former officials said, or because the receiving country has limited the number of people it can accept.

Recent deportation flights to the Haitian coastal city of Cap Haitien have carried as few as 57 people, according to the Human Rights First advocacy group.

(Reporting by Kristina Cooke in San Francisco and Ben Kellerman in ​New York; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage and Alistair Bell)

text:
While US President Donald Trump publicly joked about giant reptiles devouring would-be escapees from the now-shuttered Alligator Alcatraz immigrant detention center in the Florida Everglades, a newly published report by the Department of Homeland Security's internal watchdog confirms that the biggest dangers facing detainees at the notorious lockup were found inside its walls.

The DHS Office of Inspector General (OIG) found that staff at Alligator Alcatraz—officially called the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF)—"complied with intake and use-of-force standards but did not comply with standards related to environmental health and safety, special management units, medical care, food service, personal hygiene, and recreation."

Affirming reports from human rights groups like Amnesty International, the OIG reported on September 11 that staff at the facility, which was operated by the state of Florida and private contractors, "confined 79 detainees in small metal enclosures—each offering about 18 square feet of floor space—for periods ranging from several minutes to nearly two hours."

"Facility staff described the small metal enclosures as 'calming areas' for detainees to de-escalate and have time alone," the report states. "Staff further maintained that detainees asked to spend time in the small metal enclosures. We found at least one instance in which the small metal enclosures may have been used as a disciplinary tool."

While held in the cages, detainees—who reported being shackled and locked to the ground—were subjected to dangerously high temperatures and swarms of mosquitoes. Amnesty described the use of the cages as a form of torture.

"Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among detention facilities OIG has inspected and presents significant risks to detainee health and safety," the DHS report notes.

Responding to the report's findings, Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) said on social media that "this is nothing short of torture."

"DHS needs to be dismantled and held accountable for this complete inhumanity," she added.

The OIG report additionally found that "FSSF did not provide detainees with sufficient living space, creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units, which may harm detainees’ physical and mental health."

According to the OIG, detainees had about 28 square feet of living space each when the facility was at maximum capacity, well below the 75-square-foot DHS benchmark.

Three-quarters of the detainees interviewed by the OIG said they did not have access to clean drinking water.

The OIG also found that detainees were generally permitted to shower just three times a week, and inspectors noted insects in the showers.

Detainee recreation was also limited to three one-hour sessions per week.

The OIG report ominously concludes that "although FSSF ceased operations in June 2026, the issues raised by the department’s

management response regarding [US Immigration and Customs Enforcement's] level of oversight and responsibility for immigration detention remain consequential."

The publication cites the Baker Correctional Institution—also known as "Deportation Depot"—in Sanderson, Florida, which has yet to undergo OIG inspection, and where detainees and their advocates have reported abuses and inhumane conditions similar to those alleged at Alligator Alcatraz.

Some critics of the new OIG report denounced what they said were critical omissions and falsehoods, including that FSSF complied with use-of-force standards. Clients of attorney Katherine Blankenship and other detainees at the facility said they were beaten—and one man had his wrist fractured—after complaining about not having phone access earlier this year.

The Associated Press reported in April:

When one detainee approached a guard, he was punched in the face. The guards then started beating other detainees in the cell. One of Blankenship’s clients was punched in the right eye, thrown to the floor, and beaten by several guards. He was kicked in the head and his shoulder and arm were injured. A guard put his knee on the detainee’s neck while restraining him, according to the attorney’s declaration, which included a photo made during a video call almost a week later showing the detainee with a bruised eye.

Other alleged abuses and inhumane conditions at Alligator Alcatraz not mentioned in the OIG report include rotten and maggot-infested food, 24-hour lighting, flooding, and denial of religious practice.

Some detainees also claimed they were held in the phone booth-sized cages for far longer than two hours.

“People ended up in the ‘box’ just for asking the guards for anything," one former detainee told Amnesty. "I saw a guy who was put in it for an entire day."

Responding to the new OIG report, Congressman Adam Smith (D-Wash.) said Monday on social media that "people at Florida's Alligator Alcatraz were subjected to inhumane, unjust punishment, risking their health and safety while in federal detention. No person should be locked into an 18-square-foot cage, period."

Last year, Jayapal and Smith introduced the Dignity for Detained Immigrants Act, which Jayapal's office described as "legislation to enact guardrails and oversight on immigration detention, and to ensure civil and human rights are protected."

Since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, more than 50 people have died in ICE custody, including detainees who died inside lockups, during transfers, and in hospitals while still under DHS control. The agency also announced earlier this year that it would stop reporting the deaths of people recently released from ICE detention.

Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, President and CEO of the advocacy group Global Refuge, said in a statement responding to the new OIG report that "there is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a 'calming area' is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike."

"The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food, and basic hygiene—and in at least one case locked in a cage as punishment," Vignarajah continued. "That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty, carried out in our name and on our dime, to the tune of more than a million dollars a day."

"The facility is closed, but the mindset that built it lives on," she added. "We cannot let Alligator Alcatraz become a blueprint. We call on Congress and the Department of Homeland Security to guarantee that no one held in the United States—regardless of where they were born or how they arrived—is subjected to conditions this administration's own watchdog has deemed inhumane."
